docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
An example of a client/server [React] / [NestJS]

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude, reviewed by Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course builds, step by step, a complete client/server application for booking medical appointments, RdvMedecins: a NestJS server written in TypeScript that exposes a JSON API, a MySQL database and a React 19 client that consumes this API.

On the server side, it sets up the working environment, presents NestJS, then builds the application’s server with TypeORM and MySQL, JWT authentication (@nestjs/passport, @nestjs/jwt) and role-based access control.

On the client side, it introduces React (function components, hooks), then builds the application’s client with Vite and TypeScript, a Bootstrap interface and French and English internationalization with i18next.

Prerequisites: no knowledge of NestJS or React is required. You only need the basics of JavaScript, HTTP exchanges (GET, POST, JSON), HTML and the command line.

This course ports the 2014 course A Client/Server Example - AngularJS 1.x / Spring 4 to current technologies. The same application is built with other clients in the Angular / NestJS, Vue.js / NestJS and Flutter / NestJS courses. To learn React from small examples, see the course Step-by-Step Introduction to the React Web Framework.

2.1. Install the tools
docs.text:
1. Node.js: Download and install version 22 (or later) from nodejs.org. Verify the installation in a terminal: 
    node --version
npm --version
  1. Visual Studio Code (VSCode): available for free download from code.visualstudio.com. Install the “TypeScript and JavaScript Language Features” extension (usually already included).
  2. [NestJS] CLI, installed once and for all (on the client side; [Vite] does not require any global installation—see introduction). In a VSCode terminal: 
    npm install -g @nestjs/cli
  1. [MySQL] 8: Install, for example, via XAMPP, Laragon (on Windows), or directly via [MySQL] Community Server. A graphical administration tool (phpMyAdmin, [MySQL] Workbench, DBeaver, HeidiSQL…) simplifies the process. Subsequently, the Laragon tool is used.
  2. Postman: available for free download at postman.com.

If you have downloaded the code, it is located in two folders:

  • in [1], the client is [React];
  • in [2], the server [NestJS];

Open the [2] folder with Visual Studio [File / Open Folder]:

docs.title: 2.2. Create the database
docs.text:
To create the [MySQL] database used by the [NestJS] server, we will use the Laragon tool. As of September 2026, Laragon is available at URL [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment ]. Laragon includes tools that allow you to install a PHP server and the [MySQL] DBMS server:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • into [2], the [MySQL] DBMS;
  • to [3], a messaging tool that we will not be using;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, [MySQL], MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for URL [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used by the [NestJS] server;
  • In [7], open a terminal; all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • In [8], open a Windows Explorer window in the folder associated with URL [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

  • In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:
  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • in [3], a [git] client that allows you to manage different versions of a project;
  • in [4], a database manager;
  • [5], a mail manager;
  • in [6], the [MySQL] DBMS;
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will use only the [MySQL] DBMS [6] and [heidisql] to manage it graphically;

To create the [MySQL] database required by the [NestJS] server, proceed as follows:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • In [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The option [Database] launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various DBMS options. The default value provided is MySQL. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;
  • In [1-2], run the SQL file, then select the [dbrdvmedecins.sql] file, which you’ll find in the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server/database] folder:

Running the [3] file will create the [dbrdvmedecins] database used by the [NestJS] server. To view it, run F5 within HeidiSQL to refresh the display:

The database [dbrdvmedecins] has been created. You can view its contents:

  • In [1-3], the table [clients];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the row’s version number. This number increments each time the row is modified;
    • [title, last_name, first_name] identifies the person;

  • in [1-3], the table [doctors];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the version number of the row;
    • [title, last_name, first_name] identifies the person;

  • In [1-3], the table [slots] of doctors’ appointment time slots:
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: row version number;
    • [doctor_id]: foreign key referencing the doctor’s primary key;
    • [start_hour, start_minute]: hour and minutes of the appointment start time. Thus, [8,20] means 8:20 a.m.
    • [end_hour, end_minute]: hour and minutes of the end of the consultation.

  • In [1-3], the [appointments] table of scheduled appointments;
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: version number;
    • [day]: appointment date;
    • [slot_id]: foreign key referencing the primary key of the appointment time slot. Since a time slot is linked to a doctor, we know which doctor is handling this appointment;
    • [client_id]: foreign key to the number (primary key) of the patient attending the appointment;

  • in [1-3], the table [users] lists the users authorized to use the application [NestJS];
    • [id, version]: primary key, version number;
    • [login, password]: user credentials;
    • [name]: user name;
    • [role]: the user’s role. [ADMIN] has full access rights. [USER] has read-only access. This user can view a doctor’s schedule but cannot schedule or cancel an appointment;

docs.title: 2.3. Start the [NestJS] server for the first time
docs.text:
In the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder, type the following commands in a terminal:

npm install
cp .env.example .env

The [.env] file sets environment variables:

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sample configuration file.
# Copy this file to [.env] then adapt the values to your machine.
# The [.env] file must never be shared or committed (passwords).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

# listening port of the NestJS server (the original Spring server listened on 8080)
PORT=8080

# connection parameters for the MySQL database [dbrdvmedecins]
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_DATABASE=dbrdvmedecins

# in development only: TypeORM can automatically create/update
# the tables from the entities. It is disabled here because we provide our
# own SQL script [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql], as the original Spring project did.
DB_SYNCHRONIZE=false

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# authentication (see src/auth/)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# secret key used to sign/verify JWT tokens - MUST be changed
# in production (a long random string, never committed).
JWT_SECRET=change-me-to-a-long-random-string
# validity of a JWT token (see the documentation of the [ms] library:
# "60", "2h", "7d"...)
JWT_EXPIRES_IN=2h

Customize the newly created file [.env] to match your [MySQL] installation (username, password, port). Since authentication was added (see Chapter 3), this file also contains a key named JWT_SECRET: the example value is suitable for following along with this document, but must be replaced with a unique random string of your own before any actual use.

Start all Laragon services [Start All], if you haven’t already done so.

Then start the server:

npm run start:dev

The console displays, in order: the startup of the [NestJS] module, the list of routes exposed by the controller, and then the startup confirmation:

docs.title: 2.4. Testing the Server with a Browser
docs.text:
Since authentication was added (Chapter 3), all routes in [RdvMedecinsController] require a valid JWT token: therefore, a browser alone can no longer be used to test them directly. For example:

http://localhost:[8080/getAllDoctors]

now returns a 401 Unauthorized error without a token:

This is the expected behavior: this response confirms that the server is properly protecting its routes. Postman (next section) is required to obtain a token and then use it.

docs.title: 2.5. Testing the [NestJS] server with Postman
docs.text:
The Postman tool is available at URL [https://www.postman.com/downloads/]. You may need to create an account.

Start all Laragon services, then open the Postman desktop application:

  • In [1-2], create a request HTTP to query the doctors’ appointment management server;

docs.title: 2.5.1. Log in and obtain a token
docs.text:
1. Create a new Postman request with the method POST, URL http://localhost:8080/login;
  2. In the [Body] tab, select "raw," then the JSON format, and enter: {"login": "admin", "password": "admin"} (or "user/user" to test the USER role);
  3. Submit the request.
  • in [1-2], the request POST to the server [NestJS] running on port 8080;
  • to [3-5], the body of the request. This transmits to the server the string JSON containing the credentials of the user attempting to log in, in this case admin/admin;
  • in [6], the server’s response;
  • in [7], the authentication token that subsequent requests must send to the server to indicate “I have already authenticated”;

Copy the value from accessToken: this is the token you must now include in every subsequent request. In the example above, the token to copy is “eyJ...zoM” (without the quotes).

docs.title: 2.5.2. Calling a protected route with the token
docs.text:
For GET /getAllDoctors (or any other route starting with RdvMedecinsController), in Postman, on the Authorization tab, select the Bearer Token type and paste the token copied above (Postman will then automatically add the Authorization: Bearer <token> header).

  • in [1-2], the request sent to the server. It requests the list of doctors in the database;
  • In [3-5], the request must send the authentication token. In [4], select [Bearer Token], and in [5], paste the authentication token you copied earlier;
  • in [7], the server’s response;

In Postman, press Ctrl-0 to load the collection:

To test /addAppointment with the token from an account ADMIN:

  1. Postman request, method POST, URL http://localhost:8080/addAppointment;
  2. Authorization tab: Bearer Token, admin token;
  3. [Body] tab, raw, JSON: {"day": "2026-09-13", "clientId": 1, "slotId": 5};
  4. Submit the request.

You can verify with HeidiSQL that an appointment has been added to the database:

To test /deleteAppointment, follow the same procedure with the body {"appointmentId": 2} (the ID of the appointment to be canceled (8) above).

  • in [4], where the number above is the appointment to be deleted;

  • to [5-7], the authentication token;
  • to [9], the server’s response. [status=0] indicates that the operation was successful. You can verify this with HeidiSQL:

Try this: repeat the same request /addAppointment using the token for the USER account (user/user) instead of the admin token: the response becomes 403 Forbidden, with the message “role [USER] does not allow this action (required role: ADMIN)”—a concrete demonstration of the role-based access control implemented in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 2.6. Launch the [React] client for the first time
docs.text:
In the rdvmedecins-react-client folder (the [NestJS] server must be started beforehand):

npm install
npm start

Then open http://localhost:4200 in a browser: the login screen appears first (see Chapter 5).

  • in [1], the URL server that serves the [React] application;
  • to [2], the URL of the server [NestJS] that manages the database [dbrdvmedecins];

It is important to understand that there are two web servers here, one of which acts as a client to the other.

Two buttons labeled “FR” and “EN” in the upper-right corner allow you to switch the interface to French (it is displayed in English by default, or in French if the browser is set to French), even before logging in. Log in with one of the two demo accounts (admin/admin, full access, or user/user, read-only) to access the rest of the application. Chapter 5 provides a detailed guide to using this client, with screenshots for each step.

docs.title: 3.1. Sources
docs.text:
This chapter draws on the following sources:

  • the official [NestJS] website: nestjs.com and its documentation docs.nestjs.com;
  • the framework’s GitHub repository: github.com/nestjs/nest.

docs.title: 3.2. The role of [NestJS] in a web application
docs.text:
[NestJS] is a Node.js framework written in TypeScript, designed to build the server-side of a web application —most often a API REST (JSON). It does not reinvent the HTTP protocol handling itself: by default, it relies on Express, a more rudimentary Node.js framework responsible for receiving raw HTTP requests and responding to them. [NestJS] sits on top of this, providing a code organization that neither Node.js nor Express imposes on their own: division into modules, controllers, and services; dependency injection; decorators…

Its architecture is heavily inspired by [Angular] (decorators, modules, dependency injection)—a similarity that readers of the [Angular] version of this course will find again on the client side.

[NestJS] is primarily designed to generate JSON responses: by default, whatever a controller method returns is automatically converted to JSON and sent to the client, without any special configuration.

docs.title: 3.3. The [NestJS] Development Model
docs.text:
Three concepts form the structure of a [NestJS] application:

  • modules (@[Module] decorator): A module groups together a set of interrelated features—it declares which controllers and services belong to it, which other modules it requires, and what it makes available to others. A [NestJS] application always starts from a root module, [AppModule], which assembles all the other modules in the project;
  • controllers (@[Controller] decorator): A controller is the application’s entry point—a class in which each method receives HTTP requests corresponding to a specific URL, and returns a response to the client;
  • providers (decorator @[Injectable]): a provider is a regular class, typically responsible for business logic or data access, which [NestJS] can automatically create and provide (i.e., “inject”) to any controller or service that needs it.

In practice, a class that needs a provider simply declares it as a parameter in its constructor—[NestJS] creates the necessary instance and passes it automatically, without ever having to write new yourself: this is called constructor-based dependency injection, a practice that is almost always used in NestJS.

docs.title: 3.4. A first example: the “hello” mini-project
docs.text:
To reinforce these three concepts, here’s a very small [NestJS] project, independent of the case study (a single route /hello), which you could create with (type these commands into an empty folder that you’ve opened in VSCode [File/Open Folder]. These commands create a folder named [hello-nest]):

npm install -g [@nestjs/cli]
nest new hello-nest
cd hello-nest
npm run start:dev

This command generates a project containing the following essential files: [src/main.ts], src/app.module.ts, src/app.controller.ts, src/app.service.ts. These four files alone illustrate the architecture of a [NestJS] application: an entry point ([main.ts]), a root module (app.module.ts), a controller (app.controller.ts), and a service (app.service.ts).

docs.title: 3.4.1. The service
docs.text:
// src/app.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class AppService {
  getHello(): string {
    return 'Hello World!';
  }
}
  • line 2: each element used is explicitly imported; here, [Injectable] is imported from [@nestjs/common], the module that contains most of the decorators and utility classes from [NestJS];
  • line 4: A decorator is an annotation placed immediately above a class, method, or parameter TypeScript (preceded by the @ symbol), which modifies or enhances its behavior without altering its code—the mechanism upon which virtually the entire NestJS vocabulary is based. @[Injectable]() marks this class as a provider: [NestJS] will create it on its own and automatically provide it to any other class that requests it in its constructor, without ever having to write new [AppService]();
  • Line 6: : string declares the return type—a feature specific to TypeScript that is absent in JavaScript.

docs.title: 3.4.2. The controller
docs.text:
// src/app.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppService } from './app.service.js';

@Controller()
export class AppController {
  constructor(private readonly appService: AppService) { }

  @Get('hello')
  getHello(): string {
    return this.appService.getHello();
  }
}
  • Line 5: @Controller() decorates the following class to make it a controller: NestJS will send it the HTTP requests corresponding to its routes. The argument in parentheses is an optional prefix added to the beginning of all the class’s routes—here it is empty: the “hello” route therefore responds directly to /hello;
  • line 7: the constructor declares a parameter appService of type [AppService], preceded by the modifier TypeScript private readonly, which, in a single line, declares it and registers it as a property of the instance (`this.appService`). [NestJS] determines that the controller needs a [AppService], creates an instance of it (a single instance, shared by the entire application), and automatically provides it here: this is the constructor-based dependency injection mentioned earlier;
  • Line 9: [@Get]('hello') associates the following method with the route HTTP GET /hello: This decorator makes the action accessible at the testable address http://localhost:3000/hello once the server is running. Other decorators serve the same purpose for the other HTTP verbs: @[Post](), @Put(), @Delete(), @Patch() (we’ll use @[Post]() in the case study, for /addAppointment and /deleteAppointment). Note that on line 10, the method name [getHello] is irrelevant. It could be any name;
  • line 11: the controller delegates the work to the injected service rather than coding the response itself: it remains a simple routing layer, while the business logic resides in the service—a principle we’ll see, on a larger scale, in the case study in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 3.4.3. The module
docs.text:
// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppController } from './app.controller.js';
import { AppService } from './app.service.js';

@Module({
  imports: [],
  controllers: [AppController],
  providers: [AppService],
})
export class AppModule {}
  • line 6: @[Module]({...}) decorates the following class to turn it into a module: it groups a coherent part of the application and declares, in the object passed as an argument, what comprises it. Four properties are possible: controllers (the controllers exposed by this module), providers (the services provided by this module, available for injection within the module), imports (the other modules on which this one depends), and exports (the providers that this module makes available to modules that import it);
  • Without the `controllers: [AppController]` line, `[NestJS]` would ignore this controller, and its routes would not respond to any requests; without `providers: [AppService]`, the controller’s dependency injection would fail at startup.

docs.title: 3.5. Providers and Dependency Injection
docs.text: A class annotated with @[Injectable]() is a provider: [NestJS] knows how to instantiate it and automatically inject it wherever it is requested in a constructor, provided it appears in a module’s providers array. By default, a [NestJS] provider is a singleton: a single instance is created when the application starts, and that same instance is shared by all components that need it—an important point for understanding the role of the [ApplicationModelService] service in the case study (Chapter 3), which caches data when the server starts.

docs.title: 3.6. The other decorators that will appear in the case study
docs.text:
DecoratorRole 
[@Get](url), [@Post](url)
associates a controller method with a route HTTP 
[@Param]('x')
retrieves a variable segment from URL, e.g., /getDoctorById/:id 
[@Body]()
retrieves the body JSON of a request POST, deserialized into a class 
[@Injectable]()
declares a provider (service, DAO…) 
[@Module]({...})
declares a module, an assembly of controllers and providers

These decorators will be explained in detail, one by one, at the exact location where they appear in the code of the [RdvMedecins] server (Chapter 3).

It follows the same format used throughout this course: the source code, numbered line by line, followed by a section titled “Let’s Comment on This Code,” which explains the lines that require further clarification. docs.title: 4.1. The database
docs.text: The structure of the [dbrdvmedecins] database mirrors that of the original document (2014, Spring 4 / [MySQL] 5): the same tables—[doctors], [clients], [slots], [appointments]—the same foreign keys, and the same uniqueness constraint. The only new addition, introduced by the “authentication” step of this port: the table [users].

docs.title: 4.1.1. [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql]
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
  -- Database [dbrdvmedecins] - MySQL 8
  --
  -- This script reproduces EXACTLY the relational schema of the original document
  -- (2014, Spring 4 / Spring Data / MySQL 5): same tables, same columns,
  -- same foreign keys, same uniqueness constraint. Only the database engine
  -- changes its name (MySQL 5 -> MySQL 8), not the structure.
  --
  -- The [users] table now appears ("authentication" step of this
 -- port). The original document used THREE tables (users, roles,
 -- users_roles) to allow a user to have SEVERAL roles.
 -- Since this application only knows two mutually exclusive roles
 -- (ADMIN, USER), we simplify here to a single [role] column
 -- on the [users] table rather than rebuilding the original many-to-
 -- many relation - a deliberate teaching simplification, documented
 -- in the "Authentication" chapter of the course.
 -- =========================================================================

 -- we start again from an empty database on each run of the script (handy in development)
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS appointments;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS slots;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS doctors;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

 CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
 USE dbrdvmedecins;

 CREATE TABLE doctors (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
   last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
   first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
 );

 CREATE TABLE clients (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
   last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
   first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
 );

 CREATE TABLE slots (
   id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   doctor_id    INT NOT NULL,
   start_hour   INT NOT NULL,
   start_minute INT NOT NULL,
   end_hour     INT NOT NULL,
   end_minute   INT NOT NULL,
   CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY (doctor_id) REFERENCES doctors(id)
 );

 CREATE TABLE appointments (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   day        DATE NOT NULL,
   slot_id    INT NOT NULL,
   client_id  INT NOT NULL,
   CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_slot   FOREIGN KEY (slot_id)   REFERENCES slots(id),
   CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_client FOREIGN KEY (client_id) REFERENCES clients(id),
   CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)
 );

 CREATE TABLE users (
   id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
   password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
   name     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
   role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL
 );

   (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), /* ... */ (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

   (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), /* ... */ (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

 INSERT INTO appointments (day, slot_id, client_id) VALUES (CURDATE(), 2, 3);

 INSERT INTO users (login, password, name, role) VALUES
   ('admin', '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrator', 'ADMIN'),
   ('user',  '$2b$10$6Cvoion7AgJkpYHw5N0jMuWPf8T90J28En56kWBL9PT0bXt7lwW7.', 'User',          'USER');

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 20–24: [DROP TABLE IF EXISTS …] — the script starts with an empty database on each execution, in the reverse order of dependencies (starting with `appointments`, which references `[slots]` and `clients`, all the way down to `users`, which is not referenced by anyone): [MySQL] would refuse to delete a table still referenced by a foreign key;
  • line 48: [doctor_id INT NOT NULL], then line 53: [CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY …] — a time slot always belongs to a doctor;
  • line 64: [CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)] — the application’s central business rule: the same time slot on the same day can be booked only once. It is this constraint, and this constraint alone, that prevents a duplicate appointment—neither the validator nor the business logic layer explicitly rechecks it (see below, addAppointment);
  • lines 67–74: [CREATE TABLE users (…)] — the table added by this step. `login` is UNIQUE (two users cannot share the same login ID); `password` stores a password hashed using bcrypt (never in plaintext); role is either 'ADMIN' or 'USER'—a simple text column, whereas the original document used three tables (users, roles, users_roles) to allow multiple roles per user. Since this application requires only two mutually exclusive roles, the original many-to-many relationship would have been more than necessary;
  • lines 91–93: [INSERT INTO users …] — two demo accounts, admin/admin (role ADMIN) and user/user (role USER), with their passwords already hashed using bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)—never in plaintext, including in this demo script.

docs.title: 4.2. Layered Organization
docs.text:
The server follows the layered structure of the original project:

Each layer communicates only with the layer immediately to its right, [5-8]: thus, the controller [5] never communicates directly with layer [7], for example. This follows the same design principle as the original Spring project, and it makes each layer replaceable independently of the others.

docs.title: 4.3. The [TypeORM] entities (src/entities/)
docs.text: Entities are the classes that represent database table rows as TypeScript objects—the direct equivalent of the JPA entities from the original project (package rdvmedecins.entities).

docs.title: 4.3.1. src/entities/abstract.entity.ts
docs.text:
import { [PrimaryGeneratedColumn], [VersionColumn] } from 'typeorm';

  export abstract class AbstractEntity {
    @PrimaryGeneratedColumn()
    id: number;

    @VersionColumn()
    version: number;
  }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 4: [@PrimaryGeneratedColumn()] — declares an auto-incrementing primary key using the DBMS - the exact equivalent of @Id + @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.AUTO) in JPA;
  • Line 7: [@VersionColumn()] — [TypeORM]’s native mechanism for optimistic locking: [TypeORM] automatically increments this column with every modification and raises an error if you attempt to save an entity whose version no longer matches the one in the database (someone else has modified it in the meantime) - the exact equivalent of @Version in JPA/Hibernate;
  • Line 3: [export abstract class AbstractEntity {] — this class is not decorated by [@Entity]: it does not correspond to any table on its own. [TypeORM] refers to this technique as “Concrete Table Inheritance”: each subclass decorated with [@Entity] gets its own table, with all inherited columns—the exact equivalent of @MappedSuperclass in JPA.

docs.title: 4.3.2. src/entities/person.entity.ts
docs.text:
import { [Column] } from 'typeorm';
  import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';

  export abstract class Person extends AbstractEntity {
    @Column({ length: 5 })
    title: string;

    @Column({ name: 'last_name', length: 20 })
    lastName: string;

   @Column({ name: 'first_name', length: 20 })
   firstName: string;
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 4: [export abstract class Person extends AbstractEntity {] — groups the fields common to both a doctor and a patient (title, last name, first name), while inheriting id/version ([AbstractEntity]). Like its parent class, it is not decorated by [@Entity]: it is the counterpart ([TypeORM]) to the class [Personne]—which is also @MappedSuperclass—from the original project;
  • Lines 5, 8, 11: [@Column({ length: N })] / [@Column({ name: '...', length: N })] — three columns of text of fixed length (with an explicit snake_case column name, last_name / first_name, for the last two), equivalent to [@Column](length = N) private String ... in JPA.

docs.title: 4.3.3. src/entities/doctor.entity.ts
docs.text:
import { [Entity], [OneToMany] } from 'typeorm';
  import { Person } from './person.entity';
  import { Slot } from './slot.entity';

  @Entity({ name: 'doctors' })
  export class Doctor extends Person {
    @OneToMany(() => Slot, (slot) => slot.doctor)
    slots: Slot[];
  }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 5: [@Entity({ name: 'doctors' })] — declares the class as the [TypeORM] entity, persisted in the table [doctors]—the exact equivalent of [@Entity] + @Table(name = "[doctors]") in JPA;
  • line 6: [export class Doctor extends Person {] — inherits title/lastName/firstName (from [Person]) and id/version (from [AbstractEntity]), without having to redeclare them;
  • line 7: [@OneToMany(() => Slot, (slot) => slot.doctor)] — declares the inverse relationship “a doctor has multiple time slots”: a navigation convenience feature, absent from the original project (which declared it only in the other direction, on the [Creneau] side), but easy to add with TypeORM.

docs.title: 4.3.4. src/entities/client.entity.ts
docs.text:
import { [Entity] } from 'typeorm';
  import { Person } from './person.entity';

  @Entity({ name: 'clients' })
  export class Client extends Person {}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 4–5: [@Entity({ name: 'clients' }) export class Client extends Person {}] — exactly the same principle as [Doctor], with no additional relationships: a table [clients], with the same three columns inherited from Person. Vocabulary reminder: [Client] refers here to a patient at the medical practice (vocabulary from the original business domain), not to be confused with “client HTTP.”

docs.title: 4.3.5. src/entities/slot.entity.ts
docs.text:
import { [Column], [Entity], [JoinColumn], [ManyToOne], [RelationId] } from 'typeorm';
  import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
  import { Doctor } from './doctor.entity';

  @Entity({ name: 'slots' })
  export class Slot extends AbstractEntity {
    @Column({ name: 'start_hour' }) startHour: number;
    @Column({ name: 'start_minute' }) startMinute: number;
    @Column({ name: 'end_hour' }) endHour: number;
   @Column({ name: 'end_minute' }) endMinute: number;

   @ManyToOne(() => Doctor, (doctor) => doctor.slots)
   @JoinColumn({ name: 'doctor_id' })
   doctor: Doctor;

   @RelationId((slot: Slot) => slot.doctor)
   doctorId: number;
 }

Let’s break down this code:

  • lines 7–10: [@Column({ name: 'start_hour' }) startHour: number; …] — the four time boundaries of the appointment slot (start and end hour/minute), four single integers, each mapped to its snake_case column (start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute);
  • line 12: [@ManyToOne(() => Doctor, (doctor) => doctor.slots)] — multiple time slots belong to the same doctor. By default, [TypeORM] does not load the “doctor” relationship when reading a time slot (default “lazy” behavior): you must request it explicitly (option relations: ['doctor'] in a query)—exactly as FetchType.LAZY required, on the JPA side, an explicit `left join fetch` in the JPQL query to retrieve the doctor;
  • line 13: [@JoinColumn({ name: 'doctor_id' })] — specifies the name of the foreign key column in table [slots];
  • line 16: [@RelationId((slot: Slot) => slot.doctor)] — the exact and idiomatic equivalent, on the [TypeORM] side, of the read-only field idMedecin in the original project ([@Column](name = "id_medecin", insertable = false, updatable = false)): it directly exposes the foreign key value, without needing to load the entire [Doctor] entity—useful for building lightweight JSON responses (see below, the web layer).

Note: A [@RelationId] field is a virtual column, calculated after the fact by [TypeORM] —it is not a true SQL column that can be used in a WHERE clause of a “query builder” (see below, [SlotRepository]). It is used solely to retrieve the foreign key value once the entity has been loaded.

docs.title: 4.3.6. src/entities/appointment.entity.ts
docs.text:
import { [Column], [Entity], [JoinColumn], [ManyToOne], [RelationId], [Unique] } from 'typeorm';
  import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';
  import { Client } from './client.entity';
  import { Slot } from './slot.entity';

  @Entity({ name: 'appointments' })
  @Unique('unq1_appointments', ['day', 'slot'])
  export class Appointment extends AbstractEntity {
    @Column({ type: 'date' })
   day: string;

   @ManyToOne(() => Client)
   @JoinColumn({ name: 'client_id' })
   client: Client;

   @ManyToOne(() => Slot)
   @JoinColumn({ name: 'slot_id' })
   slot: Slot;

   @RelationId((appointment: Appointment) => appointment.client)
   clientId: number;

   @RelationId((appointment: Appointment) => appointment.slot)
   slotId: number;
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 7: [@Unique('unq1_appointments', ['day', 'slot'])] — refers, on the [TypeORM] side, to the constraint SQL in the database script. Note: Here, we are referencing the relation name (“slot”), not the field [@RelationId] (“slotId”)—the latter is a virtual column, which [TypeORM] does not accept in an @Unique constraint. [TypeORM] itself maps 'slot' to its actual foreign key column (slot_id);
  • line 9: [@Column({ type: 'date' })] — type 'date' (not 'datetime'): only the day is retained, not the time—exactly as TemporalType.DATE specified on the JPA side;
  • lines 12–18: [@ManyToOne(...) / @JoinColumn(...)] — two relationships, to [Client] and to [Slot], following the same principle as [slot.entity.ts];
  • lines 20–24: [@RelationId(...)] — the read-only equivalents of the idClient/idCreneau fields from the original project (same mechanism as Slot.doctorId, see above).

docs.title: 4.3.7. src/entities/user.entity.ts
docs.text:
import { [Column], [Entity] } from 'typeorm';
  import { AbstractEntity } from './abstract.entity';

  export type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'USER';

  @Entity({ name: 'users' })
  export class User extends AbstractEntity {
    @Column()
    login: string;

   @Column()
   password: string;

   @Column()
   name: string;

   @Column()
   role: Role;
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 4: [export type Role = ‘ADMIN’ | ‘USER’;] — a simple concatenation of two strings, TypeScript: the only two roles managed by the application. This type is reused everywhere else where a role is handled (roles.decorator.ts, jwt.strategy.ts, the client [React]…);
  • line 6: [@Entity({ name: 'users' })] — like the other entities, a dedicated table;
  • line 12: [password: string;] — stores a hashed (bcrypt) password, never in plaintext—see auth.service.ts;
  • line 18: [role: Role;] — a single column, rather than the many-to-many relationship (users/roles/users_roles) in the original Spring project. This application recognizes only two mutually exclusive roles (a user is either ADMIN or USER, never both): reconstructing the original relationship would have added complexity without any real benefit. This is a deliberate simplification for educational purposes, just like the enumeration `[ResponseStatus]` encountered earlier in this chapter.

docs.title: 4.4. Business objects (src/domain/)
docs.text: These classes do not correspond to any database table: they are constructed on the fly by combining several entities to represent a concept useful to the application (“Dr. Pelissier’s schedule for 09/13/2026”) but which does not need to be stored as-is. Equivalent to the same “domain” subfolder (or package) in the original project.

docs.title: 4.4.1. src/domain/doctor-day-slot.ts
docs.text:
import { [Slot] } from '[../entities/slot.entity]';
  import { Appointment } from '../entities/appointment.entity';

  export class DoctorDaySlot {
    constructor(
      public slot: Slot,
      public appointment: Appointment | null, // null if the slot is free that day
    ) {}
  }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 4: [export class DoctorDaySlot {] — associates a time slot with the appointment that may have been scheduled during that slot, for a given day;
  • lines 5–8: [constructor(public slot: Slot, public appointment: Appointment | null) {}] — the syntax [public] directly in the constructor’s parameters is a shortcut for TypeScript: it declares and initializes both properties on a single line each, without having to write [this.slot = slot] separately. [appointment] is null when the time slot is available.

docs.title: 4.4.2. src/domain/doctor-day-schedule.ts
docs.text:
import { [Doctor] } from '[../entities/doctor.entity]';
  import { DoctorDaySlot } from './doctor-day-slot';

  export class DoctorDaySchedule {
    constructor(
      public doctor: Doctor,
      public day: string, // format "yyyy-MM-dd"
      public doctorDaySlots: DoctorDaySlot[],
    ) {}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 4: [export class DoctorDaySchedule {] — a doctor’s complete schedule for a given day: the doctor in question, the day, and the list of their time slots (each marked as available or booked; see [DoctorDaySlot] above);
  • line 8: [public doctorDaySlots: DoctorDaySlot[],] — calculated by [BusinessService.getDoctorDaySchedule] (see below); it is this list that the controller converts into JSON for the client [React].

docs.title: 4.5. The DAO layer (src/repositories/)
docs.text:
The DAO layer (Data Access Object) is the only part of the project that communicates directly with TypeORM/MySQL—the equivalent of the Spring Data interfaces in the original project (package rdvmedecins.repositories).

The most important difference to understand between Spring Data and [TypeORM]: With Spring Data, all you had to do was declare an interface (extends CrudRepository<...>) to automatically get the basic methods (findAll, findOne, save, delete, etc.) - Spring itself generated a class that implemented it at startup. With [TypeORM], there is no automatic generation of an implementation from an interface: we directly inject the generic Repository<Entity> provided by [TypeORM] (via [@InjectRepository]), and we write the methods we want to expose ourselves, building on the pre-defined methods of this Repository or using the query builder for more specific queries.

docs.title: 4.5.1. src/repositories/doctor.repository.ts
docs.text:
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
  import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
  import { Doctor } from '../entities/doctor.entity';

  @Injectable()
  export class DoctorRepository {
    constructor(
      @InjectRepository(Doctor)
     private readonly repository: Repository<Doctor>,
   ) {}

   findAll(): Promise<Doctor[]> {
     return this.repository.find();
   }

   findById(id: number): Promise<Doctor | null> {
     return this.repository.findOneBy({ id });
   }
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 9: [@InjectRepository(Doctor)] — asks [NestJS] to provide the Repository<[Doctor]> automatically generated by [TypeORM] for the Doctor entity. This is equivalent to the automatic injection (@Autowired) of the implementation generated by Spring Data;
  • line 14: [return this.repository.find();] — equivalent to medecinRepository.findAll(), inherited from CrudRepository;
  • line 18: [return this.repository.findOneBy({ id });] — equivalent to medecinRepository.findOne(id); returns null if no doctor has this ID (like findOne in Spring Data, rather than throwing an exception).

docs.title: 4.5.2. src/repositories/client.repository.ts
docs.text:
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { Client } from '../entities/client.entity';

@Injectable()
export class ClientRepository {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Client)
    private readonly repository: Repository<Client>,
  ) {}

  findAll(): Promise<Client[]> {
    return this.repository.find();
  }

  findById(id: number): Promise<Client | null> {
    return this.repository.findOneBy({ id });
  }
}

This file is exactly the same in principle as [DoctorRepository] (see the explanation above), but applied to the entity [Client] (a patient).

docs.title: 4.5.3. src/repositories/slot.repository.ts
docs.text:
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
  import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
  import { Slot } from '../entities/slot.entity';

  @Injectable()
  export class SlotRepository {
    constructor(
      @InjectRepository(Slot)
     private readonly repository: Repository<Slot>,
   ) {}

   findAll(): Promise<Slot[]> {
     return this.repository.find();
   }

   findById(id: number): Promise<Slot | null> {
     return this.repository.findOneBy({ id });
   }

   getAllSlots(doctorId: number): Promise<Slot[]> {
     return this.repository
       .createQueryBuilder('s')
       .where('s.doctor = :doctorId', { doctorId })
       .orderBy('s.startHour', 'ASC')
       .addOrderBy('s.startMinute', 'ASC')
       .getMany();
   }
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 13–19: [findAll() / findById(id)] — identical to the principle already seen in [DoctorRepository];
  • line 21: [getAllSlots(doctorId: number): Promise<Slot[]> {] — a “custom” query, equivalent to the original query JPQL select c from [Creneau] c where c.medecin.[id]=?1;
  • line 23: [.createQueryBuilder(‘s’)] — the SQL alias s is named, just as [Creneau] c is named in JPQL;
  • line 24: [.where(‘s.doctor = :doctorId’, { doctorId })] — here, we are comparing the relationship itself (s.doctor), not the field [@RelationId] (s.doctorId): as noted above (slot.entity.ts), the latter is not a column that can be used in a WHERE. By comparing the relationship to a number, [TypeORM] recognizes that its foreign key is being targeted and generates the correct SQL, without a join;
  • lines 25–26: [.orderBy(‘s.startHour’, ‘ASC’).addOrderBy(‘s.startMinute’, ‘ASC’)] — sorts the time slots in chronological order, a useful addition that did not explicitly exist in the original Spring version.

docs.title: 4.5.4. src/repositories/appointment.repository.ts
docs.text:
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
  import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
  import { Appointment } from '../entities/appointment.entity';

  @Injectable()
  export class AppointmentRepository {
    constructor(
      @InjectRepository(Appointment)
     private readonly repository: Repository<Appointment>,
   ) {}

   findById(id: number): Promise<Appointment | null> {
     return this.repository.findOne({
       where: { id },
       relations: ['client', 'slot'],
     });
   }

   save(appointment: Appointment): Promise<Appointment> {
     return this.repository.save(appointment);
   }

   async deleteById(id: number): Promise<void> {
     await this.repository.delete(id);
   }

   getDoctorDayAppointments(doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<Appointment[]> {
     return this.repository
       .createQueryBuilder('appointment')
       .leftJoinAndSelect('appointment.client', 'client')
       .leftJoinAndSelect('appointment.slot', 'slot')
       .where('slot.doctor = :doctorId', { doctorId })
       .andWhere('appointment.day = :day', { day })
       .getMany();
   }
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 13–18: [findById(id) { … relations: [‘client’, ‘slot’] }] — relationships: [...] explicitly instructs [TypeORM] to also load the associated client and time slot (reminder: these relationships are in “lazy” mode by default; see slot.entity.ts) — useful for constructing the response JSON (see below, getMapForAppointment);
  • line 21: [return this.repository.save(appointment);] — equivalent to rvRepository.save(new Rv(jour, client, creneau));
  • line 25: [await this.repository.delete(id);] — equivalent to rvRepository.delete(rv.getId()) ;
  • line 28: [getDoctorDayAppointments(doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<Appointment[]> {] — equivalent to the original query JPQL SELECT rv FROM Rv rv LEFT JOIN FETCH rv.client c LEFT JOIN FETCH rv.creneau cr WHERE cr.medecin.[id]=?1 and rv.[jour]=?2 ;
  • lines 31–32: [.leftJoinAndSelect(‘appointment.client’, ‘client’) / .leftJoinAndSelect(‘appointment.slot’, ‘slot’)] — the equivalent of the LEFT JOIN FETCH of the original JPQL: retrieves, in a single query SQL, the client and time slot associated with each appointment;
  • Line 33: [.where(‘slot.doctor = :doctorId’, { doctorId })] — condition on the physician, obtained via a join on the time slot (rv.creneau.medecin.[id]=?1 in JPQL) — again, we are comparing the “doctor” relationship, not the corresponding [@RelationId] field.

docs.text:
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
  import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
  import { User } from '../entities/user.entity';

  @Injectable()
  export class UserRepository {
    constructor(
      @InjectRepository(User)

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 13: [findByLogin(login: string): Promise<User | null> {] — the only search method needed here, used by the connection (see auth.service.ts): it replaces the role-based search across three tables in the original project, which has become unnecessary since the simplification to a single column [role] (see user.entity.ts).

docs.title: 4.6. The business layer (src/business/)
docs.text: It is here, and nowhere else, that the application’s business rules reside—equivalent to the rdvmedecins.metier package in the original project.

docs.title: 4.6.1. src/business/business.interface.ts
docs.text:
import { Client } from '../entities/client.entity';
  import { Slot } from '../entities/slot.entity';
  import { Doctor } from '../entities/doctor.entity';
  import { Appointment } from '../entities/appointment.entity';
  import { DoctorDaySchedule } from '../domain/doctor-day-schedule';

  export interface IBusiness {
    getAllClients(): Promise<Client[]>;
    getAllDoctors(): Promise<Doctor[]>;
   getAllSlots(doctorId: number): Promise<Slot[]>;
   getDoctorDayAppointments(doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<Appointment[]>;
   getClientById(id: number): Promise<Client | null>;
   getDoctorById(id: number): Promise<Doctor | null>;
   getAppointmentById(id: number): Promise<Appointment | null>;
   getSlotById(id: number): Promise<Slot | null>;
   addAppointment(day: string, slot: Slot, client: Client): Promise<Appointment>;
   deleteAppointment(appointment: Appointment): Promise<void>;
   getDoctorDaySchedule(doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<DoctorDaySchedule | null>;
 }

 export const BUSINESS_TOKEN = 'IBusiness';

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 7: [export interface IBusiness {] — the business layer contract, independent of its implementation—the exact equivalent of the Java interface [IMetier] from the original project;
  • lines 8–18: eleven methods, one for each application requirement (lists, searches by ID, adding/deleting appointments, calculating the calendar);
  • line 21: [export const BUSINESS_TOKEN = ‘IBusiness’;] — we define an injection “token” (InjectionToken) to be able to inject this interface into the controller, exactly as Spring injected the business reference [IMetier] without knowing its concrete implementation class [Metier]. In TypeScript, interfaces are eliminated at compile time: so they cannot be used directly as injection tokens ([NestJS]); this workaround is necessary (see its use in app.module.ts and application-model.service.ts).

docs.title: 4.6.2. src/business/business.service.ts
docs.text:
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { IBusiness } from './business.interface';
  import { DoctorRepository } from '../repositories/doctor.repository';
  import { ClientRepository } from '../repositories/client.repository';
  import { SlotRepository } from '../repositories/slot.repository';
  import { AppointmentRepository } from '../repositories/appointment.repository';
  // ... entities and business objects imported (see above)

  @Injectable()
 export class BusinessService implements IBusiness {
   constructor(
     private readonly doctorRepository: DoctorRepository,
     private readonly clientRepository: ClientRepository,
     private readonly slotRepository: SlotRepository,
     private readonly appointmentRepository: AppointmentRepository,
   ) {}

   getAllClients(): Promise<Client[]> { return this.clientRepository.findAll(); }
   getAllDoctors(): Promise<Doctor[]> { return this.doctorRepository.findAll(); }
   getAllSlots(doctorId: number): Promise<Slot[]> {
     return this.slotRepository.getAllSlots(doctorId);
   }
   // ... 5 other simple delegation methods (same principle)

   addAppointment(day: string, slot: Slot, client: Client): Promise<Appointment> {
     const appointment = new Appointment();
     appointment.day = day;
     appointment.slot = slot;
     appointment.client = client;
     return this.appointmentRepository.save(appointment);
   }

   async deleteAppointment(appointment: Appointment): Promise<void> {
     await this.appointmentRepository.deleteById(appointment.id);
   }

   async getDoctorDaySchedule(doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<DoctorDaySchedule | null> {
     const doctor = await this.getDoctorById(doctorId);
     if (doctor === null) {
       return null;
     }
     const timeSlots = await this.getAllSlots(doctorId);
     const bookings = await this.getDoctorDayAppointments(doctorId, day);

     const hBookings = new Map<number, Appointment>();
     for (const booking of bookings) {
       hBookings.set(booking.slotId, booking);
     }

     const doctorDaySlots = timeSlots.map((slot) => {
       const appointment = hBookings.get(slot.id) ?? null;
       return new DoctorDaySlot(slot, appointment);
     });

     return new DoctorDaySchedule(doctor, day, doctorDaySlots);
   }
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 10: [export class BusinessService implements IBusiness {] — [@Injectable]() is equivalent to @Service("métier"): this class becomes a “provider” ([NestJS]) that [NestJS] can construct and inject where needed;
  • lines 11–16: [constructor(private readonly doctorRepository: …, …) {}] — injection of the four DAO instances, equivalent to the four @Autowired fields in the original project. [NestJS] chooses constructor injection here rather than field injection (as @Autowired does on a Java field): this is the recommended approach in TypeScript; it makes dependencies explicit and facilitates testing;
  • lines 18–23: most methods simply delegate to the DAO layer—no custom business logic;
  • lines 25–31: [addAppointment(…) { const appointment = new Appointment(); … }]—creates a new Appointment entity and saves it; it is the SQL unq1_appointments constraint (see above, the database script), and it alone, that prevents a duplicate reservation—no explicit check is performed here; a duplicate attempt will trigger a SQL exception, propagated by the DAO layer;
  • line 37: [async getDoctorDaySchedule(doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<DoctorDaySchedule | null> {] — the only method in the business layer that performs actual business logic (the others merely delegate): it calculates a doctor’s complete schedule for a given day. The algorithm is reproduced exactly as in the original document, in three steps;
  • line 42: [const timeSlots = await this.getAllSlots(doctorId);] — 1. Retrieve all of the doctor’s available time slots;
  • line 43: [const bookings = await this.getDoctorDayAppointments(doctorId, day);] — 2. retrieve all of the doctor’s appointments for the requested day;
  • lines 45–48: [const hBookings = new Map<number, Appointment>(); …] — these appointments are stored in a dictionary indexed by the time slot ID, so they can be quickly retrieved in the next step—equivalent to the `Map<Long, Rv> hReservations` in the original code;
  • lines 50–53: [const doctorDaySlots = timeSlots.map((slot) => { … })] — 3. For each time slot, we check whether it matches one of the found reservations: if so, it is “occupied” (we associate the found appointment with it); otherwise, it is “free” (appointment = null).

export enum ResponseStatus {
    OK = 0,
    RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND = 1,
    INVALID_DATE = 2,
    SERVER_ERROR = 3,
  }

  export class ServerResponse<T = unknown> {
    status: ResponseStatus;
   data: T | null;

   constructor(status: ResponseStatus, data: T | null) {
     this.status = status;
     this.data = data;
   }

   static ok<T>(data: T): ServerResponse<T> {
     return new ServerResponse<T>(ResponseStatus.OK, data);
   }

   static error<T = unknown>(status: ResponseStatus, data: T | null = null): ServerResponse<T> {
     return new ServerResponse<T>(status, data);
   }
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 1–6: [export enum ResponseStatus { … }] — the original Spring project used “ad hoc” numbers (0, 1, 2, 3, 4…) whose meaning varied from one controller method to another. This port takes the opportunity to consolidate all possible codes into a single enumeration, which is easier to learn and maintain: the behavior observable to the client (0 = success, anything else = failure) remains strictly the same;
  • Line 8: [export class ServerResponse<T = unknown> {] — the common response body for all JSON responses from the web service: { "status": 0, "data": ... }. New feature compared to the original: this class is generic ([ServerResponse]<T>) thanks to TypeScript, so that the data type is known at compile time (e.g., [ServerResponse]<[Doctor][]>) - The Java language of the original project did not allow this so easily with an `Object` type;
  • lines 17–19: [static ok(data: T): ServerResponse {] — a small static “factory” method, to write more readable controller code (ServerResponse.ok([doctors]) rather than new [ServerResponse](ResponseStatus.OK, [doctors]));
  • lines 21–23: [static error<T = unknown>(status: ResponseStatus, data: T | null = null): ServerResponse {] — its counterpart for error responses.

import { Slot } from '../../entities/slot.entity';
  import { Appointment } from '../../entities/appointment.entity';

  export function getErrorsForException(exception: unknown): string[] {
    const errors: string[] = [];
    let cause: unknown = exception;
    while (cause instanceof Error) {
      errors.push(cause.message);
      cause = cause.cause;
   }
   if (errors.length === 0) {
     errors.push(String(exception));
   }
   return errors;
 }

 export interface SlotJson {
   id: number; startHour: number; startMinute: number; endHour: number; endMinute: number;
 }

 export function getMapForSlot(slot: Slot | null | undefined): SlotJson | null {
   if (!slot) { return null; }
   return {
     id: slot.id, startHour: slot.startHour, startMinute: slot.startMinute,
     endHour: slot.endHour, endMinute: slot.endMinute,
   };
 }

 export function getListMapForSlots(slots: Slot[]): SlotJson[] {
   return slots.map((slot) => getMapForSlot(slot) as SlotJson);
 }

 export interface AppointmentJson {
   id: number;
   day: string;
   client: { id: number; title: string; lastName: string; firstName: string } | null;
   slot: SlotJson | null;
 }

 export function getMapForAppointment(appointment: Appointment | null | undefined): AppointmentJson | null {
   if (!appointment) { return null; }
   return {
     id: appointment.id,
     day: appointment.day,
     client: appointment.client
       ? { id: appointment.client.id, title: appointment.client.title, lastName: appointment.client.lastName, firstName: appointment.client.firstName }
       : null,
     slot: getMapForSlot(appointment.slot),
   };
 }

 export function getListMapForAppointments(appointments: Appointment[]): AppointmentJson[] {
   return appointments.map((appointment) => getMapForAppointment(appointment) as AppointmentJson);
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 4: [export function getErrorsForException(exception: unknown): string[] {] — equivalent to Static.getErreursForException (Exception exception). Java could chain exceptions (exception.getCause()) to explain “why” an exception occurred; in modern JavaScript/TypeScript (ES2022), errors also have a chain of causes, via the `cause` property;
  • lines 6–10: [while (cause instanceof Error) { … cause = cause.cause; }] — this is processed in the same way as the original Java code, by stacking each message encountered;
  • lines 17–19: [export interface SlotJson { … }] — the [Slot] entity is not returned as-is in JSON: it contains a relationship to “doctor” which, if loaded, would duplicate information already known to the client (the client already knows which doctor is being referred to; see the {doctorId} parameter in URL). We therefore construct a “custom” object containing only the fields needed for display;
  • line 21: [export function getMapForSlot(slot: Slot | null | undefined): SlotJson | null {] — equivalent to Static.getMapForCreneau([Creneau] creneau): converts an entity into a lightweight JSON object;

  • lines 33–38, 40–50, 52–54: [AppointmentJson / getMapForAppointment / getListMapForAppointments] — same principle, applied to appointments: the embedded client (appointment.client) is also reduced to only those fields needed for display.

docs.title: 4.7.6. src/web/rdvmedecins.controller.ts
docs.text:
RdvMedecinsController declares the application’s eleven routes, which intentionally mirror those in the original document (/getAllDoctors, /addAppointment…, English renderings of /getAllMedecins, /ajouterRv…) rather than “modernized” in the REST style (/doctors, /clients/:id…) - The purpose of this document is to compare the two implementations, not to modernize API.

  import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { ApplicationModelService } from './application-model.service';
  import { ServerResponse, ResponseStatus } from './models/response.model';
  import { PostAddAppointmentDto } from './models/post-add-appointment.dto';
  import { PostDeleteAppointmentDto } from './models/post-delete-appointment.dto';
  import { getErrorsForException, getListMapForSlots, getListMapForAppointments, getMapForAppointment } from './helpers/static.helper';
  // ... entities
  import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
  import { RolesGuard } from '../auth/roles.guard';
 import { Roles } from '../auth/roles.decorator';

 @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
 @Controller()
 export class RdvMedecinsController {
   constructor(private readonly application: ApplicationModelService) {}

   @Get('getAllDoctors')
   async getAllDoctors(): Promise<ServerResponse<Doctor[]>> {
     const messages = this.application.getMessages();
     if (messages !== null) {
       return new ServerResponse(ResponseStatus.SERVER_ERROR, messages as unknown as Doctor[]);
     }
     try {
       return ServerResponse.ok(await this.application.getAllDoctors());
     } catch (e) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.SERVER_ERROR, getErrorsForException(e) as unknown as Doctor[]);
     }
   }

   // ... getAllClients: same principle, on Client

   @Get('getAllSlots/:doctorId')
   async getAllSlots(@Param('doctorId') doctorId: string) {
     const id = Number(doctorId);
     const doctor = await this.application.getDoctorById(id);
     if (doctor === null) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND);
     }
     try {
       const slots = await this.application.getAllSlots(doctor.id);
       return ServerResponse.ok(getListMapForSlots(slots));
     } catch (e) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.SERVER_ERROR, getErrorsForException(e));
     }
   }

   // ... getDoctorAppointmentsOfDay/:doctorId/:day: checks isValidDate(day), then same principle

   @Get('getDoctorScheduleOfDay/:doctorId/:day')
   async getDoctorScheduleOfDay(@Param('doctorId') doctorId: string, @Param('day') day: string) {
     if (!isValidDate(day)) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.INVALID_DATE);
     }
     try {
       const schedule = await this.application.getDoctorDaySchedule(Number(doctorId), day);
       if (schedule === null) {
         return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND);
       }
       return ServerResponse.ok({
         doctor: schedule.doctor,
         day: schedule.day,
         slots: schedule.doctorDaySlots.map((s) => ({
           slot: { id: s.slot.id, startHour: s.slot.startHour, startMinute: s.slot.startMinute, endHour: s.slot.endHour, endMinute: s.slot.endMinute },
           appointment: getMapForAppointment(s.appointment),
         })),
       });
     } catch (e) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.SERVER_ERROR, getErrorsForException(e));
     }
   }

   // ... getDoctorById/:id, getClientById/:id, getSlotById/:id, getAppointmentById/:id:
   //     four similar methods, look up an entity by id, RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND otherwise

   @UseGuards(RolesGuard)
   @Roles('ADMIN')
   @Post('addAppointment')
   async addAppointment(@Body() post: PostAddAppointmentDto) {
     const client = await this.application.getClientById(post.clientId);
     if (client === null) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND);
     }
     const slot = await this.application.getSlotById(post.slotId);
     if (slot === null) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND);
     }
     try {
       const appointment = await this.application.addAppointment(post.day, slot, client);
       return ServerResponse.ok(getMapForAppointment(appointment));
     } catch (e) {
       return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.SERVER_ERROR, getErrorsForException(e));
     }
   }

   @UseGuards(RolesGuard)
   @Roles('ADMIN')
   @Post('deleteAppointment')
   async deleteAppointment(@Body() post: PostDeleteAppointmentDto) {
     const appointment = await this.application.getAppointmentById(post.appointmentId);
    if (appointment === null) {
      return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND);
    }
    try {
      await this.application.deleteAppointment(appointment);
      return ServerResponse.ok(null);
    } catch (e) {
      return ServerResponse.error(ResponseStatus.SERVER_ERROR, getErrorsForException(e));
    }
  }
 }

 function isValidDate(day: string): boolean {
   if (!/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(day)) {
     return false;
   }
   const date = new Date(`${day}T00:00:00Z`);
   return date.toISOString().slice(0, 10) === day;
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 12: [@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)] — applied to the class, protects all eleven routes of this controller at once: none are accessible without a valid JWT token (see the “Authentication” chapter below). This is equivalent to the original Spring Security rule .antMatchers("/**").hasRole("ADMIN"), except that here, the only requirement is to be authenticated (any role) - the restriction to the ADMIN role applies only to the two routes that modify data (lines 75–76 and 95–96);
  • line 13: [@Controller()] — no prefix: the routes are therefore exactly /getAllDoctors, /getAllClients, etc. This is equivalent to @RestController in Spring: each value returned by a method is automatically serialized as JSON;
  • line 15: [constructor(private readonly application: ApplicationModelService) {}] — cache/facade injection, equivalent to @Autowired private ApplicationModel application; ;
  • lines 19–22: [const messages = this.application.getMessages(); if (messages !== null) { … }] — first, we verify that the application has initialized correctly (see ApplicationModelService.onModuleInit), equivalent to `if (messages != null) { return new [Reponse](-1, messages); }`;
  • line 33: [async getAllSlots(@Param('doctorId') doctorId: string) {] — [@Param]('doctorId') retrieves the segment {doctorId} from URL, as a string (similar to @PathVariable(String) in Spring); we convert it to a number ourselves (line 34), whereas Spring would have done this automatically for a parameter declared as `long`;
  • lines 35–38: [const doctor = await this.application.getDoctorById(id); if (doctor === null) { … }] — we first retrieve the doctor to verify that it exists before proceeding further (equivalent to the private method getMedecin(id) in the original controller);
  • line 41: [return ServerResponse.ok(getListMapForSlots(slots));] — converts the list of entities [Slot] into a list of “lightweight” JavaScript objects (see static.helper.ts);
  • line 59: [return ServerResponse.ok({ doctor: …, day: …, slots: … });] — the calendar is formatted in “light” mode for JSON, following the same principles as getMapForSlot/getMapForAppointment;
  • line 75: [@UseGuards(RolesGuard)], then line 76: [@Roles('ADMIN')] — in addition to being authenticated (already required by [@UseGuards]([JwtAuthGuard]) for the class), you must have the role ADMIN here—the role USER receives a 403 Forbidden response (see roles.guard.ts). [RolesGuard] reads request.user (submitted by JwtAuthGuard/JwtStrategy): it therefore must run after [JwtAuthGuard] ([NestJS] first applies class guards, then method guards, in the order in which they appear);
  • lines 87–92: [try { const appointment = await this.application.addAppointment(…); … } catch (e) { … }] — at this point, class-validator (see [PostAddAppointmentDto]) has already verified that post.[day] is a valid date and that post.clientId/post.slotId are indeed integers. The constraint SQL unq1_appointments (day, slot_id) prevents two reservations from being made for the same time slot on the same day: a duplicate attempt will throw an exception, caught here, exactly like the SQLException from the original JDBC driver;
  • line 95: same restriction as line 75, for deleteAppointment: only the role ADMIN can cancel an appointment;
  • Line 112: [function isValidDate(day: string): boolean {] — a small local utility function, equivalent to the pair SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd") + setLenient(false) from the original code, which rejected, for example, “2026-13-40” (invalid month and day): Date.toISOString() reconstructs the date from the received string—if it differs from the input, it means the date did not exist.

docs.title: 4.8. Authentication (src/auth/)
docs.text:
This section documents the addition, at this stage of the course, of token-based authentication (JWT) and role-based access control (ADMIN/USER) - the functional equivalent of the Spring Security layer from the original document, rewritten using standard tools from the [NestJS] ecosystem: [@nestjs/passport] and @nestjs/jwt.

Two intentional differences from the original project, documented here once and for all:

  1. JWT instead of HTTP Basic. The original Spring project sent the Authorization: Basic <login:password in Base64> header with every request: the password (encoded, not encrypted) was therefore transmitted over the network with every call. This port uses a token instead: JWT (JSON Web Token). The password is presented only once, upon login (POST /login); the server then returns a signed token, which the client subsequently includes in every subsequent request (Authorization: Bearer <token> header). This is the current practice for this type of API, as already mentioned in the conclusion of the previous chapter.
  2. One role per user, a single database column, rather than the many-to-many relationship (users/roles/users_roles) in the original project—see user.entity.ts above.

An architectural point to understand before reading the code that follows: when a Guard rejects a request (401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden), the response never goes through the usual [ServerResponse]<T> envelope ({ status, data }): [NestJS] responds directly in its native JSON format, { statusCode, message, error }. This is a deliberate choice: security errors are handled before entering the controller (by a guard), whereas [ServerResponse]<T> is generated by the controller for business errors (resource not found, invalid date, etc.). The client [React] must therefore distinguish between these two types of error responses (see the following chapter, auth.interceptor.ts).

docs.title: 4.8.3. src/auth/local.strategy.ts
docs.text:
A Passport “strategy” describes how to authenticate a request. [LocalStrategy] can read a {login, password} pair from the body of a POST request and delegate the verification to AuthService. It is used only once, by the route POST /login (via [LocalAuthGuard]): all other protected routes will then use [JwtStrategy] (see below), not this one.

  import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
  import { Strategy } from 'passport-local';
  import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
  import { User } from '../entities/user.entity';

  @Injectable()
  export class LocalStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy) {
    constructor(private readonly authService: AuthService) {
     super({ usernameField: 'login', passwordField: 'password' });
   }

   async validate(login: string, password: string): Promise<User> {
     const user = await this.authService.validateUser(login, password);
     if (user === null) {
       throw new UnauthorizedException('incorrect login or password');
     }
     return user;
   }
 }

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 8: [export class LocalStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy) {] — conceptually equivalent to the AppUserDetailsService class from the original Spring Security project: “given some credentials, tell me who this user is”;
  • line 10: [super({ usernameField: ‘login’, passwordField: ‘password’ });] — by default, passport-local expects fields named “username” and “password” in the request body; here, we rename them to match our DTO ([LoginDto]), which uses “login” instead of “username”;
  • line 13: [async validate(login: string, password: string): Promise<User> {] — automatically called by Passport with the two fields extracted from the request. What it returns becomes request.user in the controller (see auth.controller.ts);
  • line 16: [throw new UnauthorizedException(‘incorrect login or password’);] — Passport automatically converts this exception into a HTTP 401 Unauthorized response, before it even reaches the controller.

docs.title: 4.8.4. src/auth/jwt.strategy.ts
docs.text:
The second Passport strategy: it can read a JWT token from the HTTP Authorization: Bearer <token> header of each request, verify its signature, and extract the user’s identity—without ever querying the database (the token already contains everything needed). This is the mechanism that protects the eleven routes of RdvMedecinsController.

  import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
  import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
  import { ExtractJwt, Strategy } from 'passport-jwt';

  export interface JwtPayload {
    sub: number;
    login: string;
    role: 'ADMIN' | 'USER';
  }

 export interface ConnectedUser {
   userId: number;
   login: string;
   role: 'ADMIN' | 'USER';
 }

 @Injectable()
 export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'jwt') {
   constructor() {
     super({
       jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),
       ignoreExpiration: false,
       secretOrKey: process.env.JWT_SECRET ?? 'dev-secret-to-change-in-production',
     });
   }

   validate(payload: JwtPayload): ConnectedUser {
     return { userId: payload.sub, login: payload.login, role: payload.role };
   }
 }

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 5–9: [export interface JwtPayload { sub: number; login: string; role: … }] — the format of the information we chose to store in the JWT token when it was generated (see auth.service.ts); sub (“subject”) is the conventional name, in JWT, for the field that contains the user’s identifier;
  • lines 11–15: [export interface ConnectedUser { … }] — what request.user will contain in the handlers once the token has been verified;
  • line 18: [export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, ‘jwt’) {] — the second argument 'jwt' names this strategy (unlike [LocalStrategy], which did not specify one): this is the name that [JwtAuthGuard] ([AuthGuard]('jwt'), see below) uses to say “use this strategy”;
  • line 21: [jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),] — the token is expected in the Authorization: Bearer xxx header;
  • line 22: [ignoreExpiration: false,] — if the token has expired, Passport rejects it (401) before even calling validate();
  • line 23: [secretOrKey: process.env.JWT_SECRET ?? ‘…’] — the secret key used to verify the token’s signature—the same one used to sign it (see auth.module.ts, which reads it from the same environment variable, JWT_SECRET);
  • line 27: [validate(payload: JwtPayload): ConnectedUser {] — automatically called by Passport once the token’s signature has been verified; converts the token’s contents to request.user.

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport';

@Injectable()
export class LocalAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('local') {}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 5: [export class LocalAuthGuard extends AuthGuard(‘local’) {}] — a “guard” ([NestJS]) determines, before a controller method is executed, whether the request is authorized to access it. [AuthGuard]('local') is a factory provided by [@nestjs/passport] that constructs a guard based on the Passport strategy named 'local' (implicitly, [LocalStrategy], which was not given an explicit name in its own constructor). This guard is used only by the route POST /login (see auth.controller.ts).

@Injectable()
