docs.title: 6.8.1. src/app/core/interceptors/auth.interceptor.ts
docs.text:
[React], being merely an interface library, does not have a built-in HTTP interceptor concept, as found in [HttpClient]/withInterceptors ([...]) on the [Angular] side. This file reimplements the same concept as a hook that encapsulates [fetch]: this is the modern equivalent of the $http interceptors from AngularJS 1.x, which were already discussed in the original document (chapter “Example 6”).

import { useAuth } from '../context/auth.context';

export function useAuthFetch() {
  const auth = useAuth();

  return async function authFetch(input: RequestInfo | URL, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<Response> {
    const headers = new Headers(init.headers);
    if (auth.accessToken) {
      headers.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${auth.accessToken}`);
    }
    const response = await fetch(input, { ...init, headers });
    if (response.status === 401) {
      auth.logOut();
    }
    return response;
  };
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 3: export function useAuthFetch() { — unlike [authInterceptor] on the [Angular] side (a function registered once and for all in [app.config.ts], which is then automatically applied to every call to [HttpClient]), [useAuthFetch()] is a hook that each caller (here, useAppointmentService(), see below) must explicitly call and use in place of fetch()—a difference in mechanism between the two libraries, not in final behavior;
  • Lines 6–10: if (auth.accessToken) { headers.set('Authorization', …); } — the direct equivalent of [request.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: … } })] on the [Angular] side. Unlike a [HttpClient] request (which is immutable), the options for [fetch] are simply a JavaScript object: there’s no need to create a “cloned” copy of it; you just need to construct the [headers] object before the call;
  • lines 12–14: if (response.status === 401) { auth.logOut(); } — same principle as on the [Angular] side (catchError + HttpErrorResponse.status === 401): a 401 during a session means the token is no longer valid, so the client is gracefully logged out; here, [fetch] does not reject its Promise with a HTTP status as an error (unlike an Observable [HttpClient])—which is why this test targets [response.status] directly, without a try/catch block;
  • line 15: return response; — the response (potentially 401) is nevertheless returned as-is to the caller, who remains responsible for handling it (see useAppointmentService(), extract<T>(), below) — the interceptor must not hide the error from the calling code.

We could manually add [Authorization: Bearer ...] to each of the methods in [useAppointmentService()]. A shared hook avoids this repetition, offering the same benefit as a [Angular] interceptor: the question “How do we authenticate a request?” is answered in a single location.

docs.title: 6.9.1. src/app/core/services/appointment.service.ts
docs.text:
Porting of [AppointmentService]: the part of the application (the ONLY one, along with [core/context/auth.context.tsx] for the connection itself) that communicates over HTTP with the [NestJS] server. This is the direct equivalent of the [dao] service presented in the chapter “Example 6: the HTTP services” in the original document (which used the AngularJS $http service).

import { useCallback } from 'react';
import { useAuthFetch } from '../interceptors/auth.interceptor';
import { useSettings } from '../context/settings.context';
import type { DoctorDaySchedule, Client, Doctor, ServerResponse, AppointmentJson } from '../models/appointment.models';

async function extract<T>(httpResponse: Response): Promise<T> {
  const envelope = (await httpResponse.json()) as ServerResponse<T>;
  if (envelope.status !== 0) {
    throw new Error(`The server answered with the error status ${envelope.status}`);
  }
  return envelope.data as T;
}

export function useAppointmentService() {
  const authFetch = useAuthFetch();
  const { apiBaseUrl } = useSettings();

  const getAllDoctors = useCallback(async (): Promise<Doctor[]> => {
    const httpResponse = await authFetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/getAllDoctors`);
    return extract<Doctor[]>(httpResponse);
  }, [authFetch, apiBaseUrl]);

  const getAllClients = useCallback(async (): Promise<Client[]> => {
    const httpResponse = await authFetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/getAllClients`);
    return extract<Client[]>(httpResponse);
  }, [authFetch, apiBaseUrl]);

  const getDoctorScheduleOfDay = useCallback(
    async (doctorId: number, day: string): Promise<DoctorDaySchedule> => {
      const httpResponse = await authFetch(
        `${apiBaseUrl}/getDoctorScheduleOfDay/${doctorId}/${day}`,
      );
      return extract<DoctorDaySchedule>(httpResponse);
    },
    [authFetch, apiBaseUrl],
  );

  const addAppointment = useCallback(
    async (day: string, clientId: number, slotId: number): Promise<AppointmentJson> => {
      const httpResponse = await authFetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/addAppointment`, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ day, clientId, slotId }),
      });
      return extract<AppointmentJson>(httpResponse);
    },
    [authFetch, apiBaseUrl],
  );

  const deleteAppointment = useCallback(
    async (appointmentId: number): Promise<void> => {
      const httpResponse = await authFetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/deleteAppointment`, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ appointmentId }),
      });
      await extract<null>(httpResponse);
    },
    [authFetch, apiBaseUrl],
  );

  return { getAllDoctors, getAllClients, getDoctorScheduleOfDay, addAppointment, deleteAppointment };
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 6: async function extract<T>(httpResponse: Response): Promise<T> { — rather than repeating, in each of the public functions, the check “if status !== 0, it’s an error,” we centralize it here just once—exactly the role of [AppointmentService.extract()] on the [Angular] side, but declared outside the hook (a regular function, so it doesn’t need to be recreated on every render);
  • line 14: export function useAppointmentService() { — a custom hook that reads and is used exactly like [inject(AppointmentService)] on the [Angular] side: it’s called once at the top of a component, then the functions it returns are used;
  • lines 18–21: const getAllDoctors = useCallback(async () => { … }, [authFetch, apiBaseUrl]); — [useCallback]() caches this function between renders, as long as [authFetch] and [[apiBaseUrl]] do not change: this optimization is necessary here because this hook is called every time the component that uses it is rendered (App.tsx)—without it, a new function [getAllDoctors] would be recreated on every render, which would unnecessarily trigger certain effects again (useEffect(…, [api]), see App.tsx below); this technical detail has no equivalent on the [Angular] side, where [AppointmentService] exists only once for the entire application (providedIn: 'root');
  • each function corresponds exactly to one of the eleven routes in the [NestJS] controller (Chapter 3)—in fact, the same names appear on both sides (getAllDoctors, addAppointment, deleteAppointment…), which makes it easier to compare the server and client sides, just as with [Angular].

Unlike [AuthService.logIn()] (previous chapter), none of the methods in this hook need to store anything after the call: it is the calling component (App.tsx) that decides what to do with the result (setDoctors(...), setSchedule(...)…) - the same separation of responsibilities as on the [Angular] side, where [AppointmentService] knows nothing about the state displayed on the screen.

docs.title: 6.10. The features layer: the four components
6.10.1. src/app/features/login/Login.tsx
docs.text:
Port of [login.component.ts/.html]: the login screen, equivalent to view [login.html] from the original client AngularJS 1.x.

import { useState, type FormEvent } from 'react';
import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';
import { useAuth } from '../../core/context/auth.context';
import './login.css';

export function Login() {
  const { t } = useTranslation();
  const auth = useAuth();

  const [login, setLogin] = useState('');
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('');
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

  async function onSubmit(event?: FormEvent): Promise<void> {
    event?.preventDefault();
    if (login.trim() === '' || password === '') {
      return;
    }
    setError(null);
    setSubmitting(true);
    try {
      await auth.logIn(login, password);
      setSubmitting(false);
    } catch {
      setSubmitting(false);
      setError('LOGIN.ERROR');
    }
  }

  return (
    <div className="row justify-content-center">
      <div className="col-sm-8 col-md-6 col-lg-4">
        <form className="card p-4" onSubmit={onSubmit}>
          <h5 className="card-title mb-3">{t('LOGIN.TITLE')}</h5>
          {error && (
            <div className="alert alert-danger py-2" role="alert">
              {t(error)}
            </div>
          )}
          <div className="mb-3">
            <label className="form-label" htmlFor="input-login">
              {t('LOGIN.LOGIN_LABEL')}
            </label>
            <input id="input-login" type="text" className="form-control"
              value={login} onChange={(e) => setLogin(e.target.value)} />
          </div>
          <div className="mb-3">
            <label className="form-label" htmlFor="input-password">
              {t('LOGIN.PASSWORD_LABEL')}
            </label>
            <input id="input-password" type="password" className="form-control"
              value={password} onChange={(e) => setPassword(e.target.value)} />
          </div>
          <button type="submit" className="btn btn-primary w-100" disabled={submitting}>
            {submitting ? t('LOGIN.SUBMITTING') : t('LOGIN.SUBMIT')}
          </button>
        </form>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 6: export function Login() { — a standalone component [Angular] declares, within its decorator [@Component], the pipes it uses (imports: [TranslatePipe]); a [React] component has nothing equivalent to declare: [useTranslation()]] (line 7) is simply imported and called, just like any other function;
  • lines 10–13: const [login, setLogin] = useState(''); … — a state that is purely local to the form (what the user is currently typing), equivalent to [signal()] local variables of the [Angular] component;
  • lines 15–16: async function onSubmit(event?: FormEvent): Promise<void> { event?.preventDefault(); — a deliberate difference from the [Angular] variant in this course: rather than listening (keyup.enter) to each field separately, this component uses a real <form> element (line 34) and its native [onSubmit] event—both the Enter key and a click on the “Log in” button (type="submit") then trigger [onSubmit()], without any additional code; [event?.preventDefault()] prevents the browser’s default behavior (reloading the page), which would violate the very principle of a Single Page Application;
  • lines 23–24: await auth.logIn(login, password); setSubmitting(false); — no further processing is needed here: [AuthContext] has already stored the session (state + localStorage)—it is App.tsx that calls useAuth().isLoggedIn, which will respond by stopping the display of <Login />;
  • lines 24–27: catch { … setError('LOGIN.ERROR'); } — an invalid username/password pair causes [logIn()] to fail with a JavaScript exception (thrown by [auth.context.tsx], see above): "LOGIN.ERROR" is displayed to the user, without attempting to distinguish between a nonexistent username and an incorrect password—exactly the same approach as in [Angular]. Storing a translation key rather than an already-resolved text has the same advantage as in [Angular]: if the user switches languages while this message is displayed, it translates itself automatically (t(error), line 38, re-evaluated on each render).

This component combines in a SINGLE .tsx file what [Angular] splits into two (login.component.ts for the logic, login.component.html for the template): the [JSX] returned by the Login() function IS the template, combined with the code TypeScript that drives it. Therefore, there is no separate .html file to comment on, unlike the equivalent chapter for the [Angular] variant of this course.

docs.title: 6.10.2. src/app/features/doctor-day-picker/DoctorDayPicker.tsx
docs.text:
Port of [doctor-day-picker.component.ts/.html]: the component that allows you to select a doctor and a day, then request to view their schedule. Conceptually equivalent to examples 7 through 10 of the original AngularJS 1.x client.

import { useState, type ChangeEvent } from 'react';
import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';
import type { Doctor } from '../../core/models/appointment.models';
import './doctor-day-picker.css';

interface DoctorDayPickerProps {
  doctors: Doctor[];
  onSearch: (criteria: { doctorId: number; day: string }) => void;
}

export function DoctorDayPicker({ doctors, onSearch }: DoctorDayPickerProps) {
  const { t } = useTranslation();
  const [selectedDoctorId, setSelectedDoctorId] = useState<number | null>(null);
  const [selectedDay, setSelectedDay] = useState<string>(
    new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10),
  );

  function onDoctorChange(event: ChangeEvent<HTMLSelectElement>): void {
    const value = event.target.value;
    setSelectedDoctorId(value === '' ? null : Number(value));
  }

  function onSearchClick(): void {
    if (selectedDoctorId === null) {
      return;
    }
    onSearch({ doctorId: selectedDoctorId, day: selectedDay });
  }

  return (
    <div className="card p-3 mb-3">
      <div className="row g-2 align-items-end">
        <div className="col-sm-5">
          <label className="form-label" htmlFor="select-doctor">
            {t('DOCTOR_DAY_PICKER.DOCTOR_LABEL')}
          </label>
          <select id="select-doctor" className="form-select" onChange={onDoctorChange}>
            <option value="">{t('DOCTOR_DAY_PICKER.CHOOSE_DOCTOR')}</option>
            {doctors.map((doctor) => (
              <option key={doctor.id} value={doctor.id}>
                {doctor.title} {doctor.firstName} {doctor.lastName}
              </option>
            ))}
          </select>
        </div>
        <div className="col-sm-4">
          <input id="input-day" type="date" className="form-control"
            value={selectedDay} onChange={(e) => setSelectedDay(e.target.value)} />
        </div>
        <div className="col-sm-3">
          <button type="button" className="btn btn-primary w-100"
            disabled={selectedDoctorId === null} onClick={onSearchClick}>
            {t('DOCTOR_DAY_PICKER.VIEW_SCHEDULE')}
          </button>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 11: export function DoctorDayPicker({ doctors, onSearch }: DoctorDayPickerProps) { — a [input.required<Doctor[]>()] [Angular] simply becomes a field of the `props` object (`doctors`); an `output<...>()` becomes a prop that contains a callback function provided by the parent `[(onSearch)]`—`[App.tsx]` will call it exactly as it subscribed to the `search` event of the `[Angular]` template;
  • lines 39–43: {doctors.map((doctor) => ( <option key={doctor.id} …>…</option> ))} — .map(...), with [key={doctor.id}], is the [React] equivalent of [@for (doctor of doctors(); track doctor.id)] on the [Angular] side: in both cases, a stable identifier specifies how to recognize a doctor that has already been displayed if it is redrawn;
  • line 37: onChange={onDoctorChange} — unlike the “login” field of [Login.tsx] (which uses [onChange] with each keystroke), a <select> only notifies when the selection actually changes—the same event HTML [change] that was already being used by [(change)="onDoctorChange($event)] on the [Angular] side.

docs.title: 6.10.3. src/app/features/schedule/Schedule.tsx
docs.text:
Port of [schedule.component.ts/.html]: displays a doctor’s schedule for a given day. Equivalent to examples 8 and 9 from the original AngularJS 1.x client. Since the addition of authentication, this component also accepts [canEdit]: when set to false (role USER), the “Book”/“Cancel” buttons disappear—the schedule remains viewable, but in read-only mode.

import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';
import type { DoctorDaySchedule, ScheduleSlot, SlotJson, AppointmentJson } from '../../core/models/appointment.models';
import './schedule.css';

interface ScheduleProps {
  schedule: DoctorDaySchedule | null;
  canEdit: boolean;
  onBook: (slot: SlotJson) => void;
  onCancel: (appointment: AppointmentJson) => void;
}

function formatTime(h: number, m: number): string {
  return `${h}:${m.toString().padStart(2, '0')}`;
}

export function Schedule({ schedule, canEdit, onBook, onCancel }: ScheduleProps) {
  const { t } = useTranslation();

  function onSlotClick(scheduleSlot: ScheduleSlot): void {
    if (!canEdit) {
      return;
    }
    if (scheduleSlot.appointment === null) {
      onBook(scheduleSlot.slot);
    } else {
      onCancel(scheduleSlot.appointment);
    }
  }

  if (schedule === null) {
    return <p className="text-muted">{t('SCHEDULE.EMPTY_STATE')}</p>;
  }

  return (
    <div className="card p-3">
      <h5>
        {t('SCHEDULE.TITLE_PREFIX')} {schedule.day} - {schedule.doctor.title} {schedule.doctor.firstName} {schedule.doctor.lastName}
      </h5>
      <table className="table table-hover align-middle">
        <thead>
          <tr><th>{t('SCHEDULE.COLUMN_SLOT')}</th><th>{t('SCHEDULE.COLUMN_STATUS')}</th><th></th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          {schedule.slots.map((scheduleSlot) => (
            <tr key={scheduleSlot.slot.id}
              className={scheduleSlot.appointment === null ? 'free-slot' : undefined}>
              <td>
                {formatTime(scheduleSlot.slot.startHour, scheduleSlot.slot.startMinute)} -{' '}
                {formatTime(scheduleSlot.slot.endHour, scheduleSlot.slot.endMinute)}
              </td>
              <td>
                {scheduleSlot.appointment === null ? (
                  <span className="badge text-bg-success">{t('SCHEDULE.FREE')}</span>
                ) : (
                  <span className="badge text-bg-secondary">
                    {scheduleSlot.appointment.client?.title} {scheduleSlot.appointment.client?.firstName} {scheduleSlot.appointment.client?.lastName}
                  </span>
                )}
              </td>
              <td>
                {canEdit && (
                  <button type="button" className={'btn btn-sm ' +
                    (scheduleSlot.appointment === null ? 'btn-outline-success' : 'btn-outline-danger')}
                    onClick={() => onSlotClick(scheduleSlot)}>
                    {scheduleSlot.appointment === null ? t('SCHEDULE.BOOK') : t('SCHEDULE.CANCEL_APPOINTMENT')}
                  </button>
                )}
              </td>
            </tr>
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 30–32: if (schedule === null) { return <p …>{t('SCHEDULE.EMPTY_STATE')}</p>; } — an early return replaces [@if (schedule(); as currentSchedule) { … } @else { … }] on the [Angular] side: a component function [React] can return any [JSX] at any point in its body, including before the end—here, as long as no search has been performed (or the agenda is empty), the function stops after displaying the empty status message, without even constructing the array;
  • line 7: canEdit: boolean; — a new feature introduced by authentication, similar to the [Angular] side: [App.tsx] passes [auth.isAdmin] to it (see below). When set to false (role USER), the “Book”/“Cancel” buttons do not even exist in DOM (see line 61, [{canEdit && (…)}])—they are not merely grayed out or disabled, but entirely absent;
  • lines 52–58: {scheduleSlot.appointment === null ? ( <span …>Free</span> ) : ( <span …>{patient name}</span> )} — the ternary operator replaces [@if (…) { … } @else { … }] on the [Angular] side: green [Bootstrap] badge (“Free”) or gray (patient’s name), depending on the slot’s status;
  • line 61: {canEdit && (…)} — the && operator displays its second operand only if the first is true (and nothing at all otherwise)—the shortest form of conditional rendering in [JSX], used here instead of the ternary operator because there is nothing to display otherwise;
  • line 65: {scheduleSlot.appointment === null ? t('SCHEDULE.BOOK') : t('SCHEDULE.CANCEL_APPOINTMENT')} — as on the [Angular] side (where a pipe can be used in any template expression), t(...) is a standard JavaScript function: it can be used directly in a ternary operator without any special syntax.

This component does not make any HTTP calls itself: it displays data received via props and notifies its parent (App.tsx) of the user’s intentions via [onBook/onCancel]—exactly the same separation of responsibilities as on the [Angular] side (book/cancel, via output()).

docs.title: 6.10.4. src/app/features/booking-dialog/BookingDialog.tsx
docs.text:
Port of [booking-dialog.component.ts/.html]: the (modal) window that allows you to select a patient to book an available slot. Equivalent to Example 9 of the original AngularJS 1.x client.

import { useState, type ChangeEvent } from 'react';
import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';
import type { Client, SlotJson } from '../../core/models/appointment.models';
import './booking-dialog.css';

interface BookingDialogProps {
  open: boolean;
  slot: SlotJson | null;
  clients: Client[];
  onConfirm: (choice: { clientId: number }) => void;
  onClose: () => void;
}

export function BookingDialog({ open, slot, clients, onConfirm, onClose }: BookingDialogProps) {
  const { t } = useTranslation();
  const [selectedClientId, setSelectedClientId] = useState<number | null>(null);

  if (!open) {
    return null;
  }

  function onClientChange(event: ChangeEvent<HTMLSelectElement>): void {
    const value = event.target.value;
    setSelectedClientId(value === '' ? null : Number(value));
  }

  function onConfirmClick(): void {
    if (selectedClientId === null) {
      return;
    }
    onConfirm({ clientId: selectedClientId });
    setSelectedClientId(null);
  }

  return (
    <>
      <div className="modal-backdrop fade show"></div>
      <div className="modal fade show d-block" tabIndex={-1} role="dialog" aria-modal="true">
        <div className="modal-dialog modal-dialog-centered">
          <div className="modal-content">
            <div className="modal-header">
              <h5 className="modal-title">{t('BOOKING_DIALOG.TITLE')}</h5>
              <button type="button" className="btn-close"
                aria-label={t('BOOKING_DIALOG.CLOSE_ARIA')} onClick={onClose}></button>
            </div>
            <div className="modal-body">
              {slot && (
                <p>
                  {t('BOOKING_DIALOG.SLOT_FROM')} {slot.startHour}:{slot.startMinute.toString().padStart(2, '0')}{' '}
                  {t('BOOKING_DIALOG.SLOT_TO')} {slot.endHour}:{slot.endMinute.toString().padStart(2, '0')}
                </p>
              )}
              <select id="select-client" className="form-select" onChange={onClientChange}>
                <option value="">{t('BOOKING_DIALOG.CHOOSE_PATIENT')}</option>
                {clients.map((client) => (
                  <option key={client.id} value={client.id}>
                    {client.title} {client.firstName} {client.lastName}
                  </option>
                ))}
              </select>
            </div>
            <div className="modal-footer">
              <button type="button" className="btn btn-secondary" onClick={onClose}>
                {t('BOOKING_DIALOG.CANCEL')}
              </button>
              <button type="button" className="btn btn-primary"
                disabled={selectedClientId === null} onClick={onConfirmClick}>
                {t('BOOKING_DIALOG.CONFIRM')}
              </button>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 18–20: if (!open) { return null; } — a [React] component can return null to display nothing at all: this is the exact equivalent of [@if (open()) { … }] on the [Angular] side (nothing is even loaded into the DOM as long as `open` is false), and of [ngIf/ngShow] in AngularJS 1.x;
  • Line 37: <div className="modal-backdrop fade show"></div> — the semi-transparent background that darkens the rest of the page—hard-coded here, whereas [Bootstrap] usually inserts it itself via JavaScript when the modal is displayed;
  • line 38: <div className="modal fade show d-block" …> — d-block replaces the role normally filled by JavaScript from [Bootstrap] (add [display:block] upon opening)—here, it is directly the conditional rendering from line 18 ([if (!open) return null;]) that plays this role;
  • line 44: aria-label={t('BOOKING_DIALOG.CLOSE_ARIA')} — unlike [attr.aria-label="'BOOKING_DIALOG.CLOSE_ARIA' | translate"] on the [Angular] side (an attribute binding distinct from the {{ }} interpolation), [JSX] makes no distinction between a HTML attribute and the content of an element: {expression} is used identically in both places.

Like the [Angular] side, this component uses the REAL classes of a modal, but its visibility is controlled by [React] (a conditional rendering based on the [open] property) rather than by the JavaScript of [Bootstrap] ([bootstrap.bundle.js, new bootstrap.Modal(...)])—to prevent [Bootstrap] and [React] from each independently managing the same information (is the modal open?), a common source of subtle bugs. The original document (2014) used a component from the angular-ui-bootstrap library (a “turnkey” modal AngularJS 1.x), which was already designed according to this same principle.

docs.title: 6.11. The root App component: orchestrator and authentication guardian
docs.text: This component fulfills the role played by the “main controller” of the original AngularJS 1.x application, and by the App component on the [Angular] side: it maintains the application’s global state and responds to events from the features/ components to call [useAppointmentService()] at the right time. Since authentication was added, it has taken on a second role: that of a “gatekeeper” on the presentation layer, which decides whether to display the login screen or the rest of the application. A [React] component combines into a single .tsx file what [Angular] splits into three ([app.ts, app.html, app.css]): the [JSX] returned by App() IS the template ([App.css] is imported below solely as a side effect).

docs.title: 6.11.1. src/app/App.tsx
docs.text:
import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';
import { useAuth } from './core/context/auth.context';
import { useSettings } from './core/context/settings.context';
import { useLanguage } from './core/context/language.context';
import { useAppointmentService } from './core/services/appointment.service';
import type { DoctorDaySchedule, Client, SlotJson, Doctor, AppointmentJson } from './core/models/appointment.models';
import { DoctorDayPicker } from './features/doctor-day-picker/DoctorDayPicker';
import { Schedule } from './features/schedule/Schedule';
import { BookingDialog } from './features/booking-dialog/BookingDialog';
import { Login } from './features/login/Login';
import './App.css';

export function App() {
  const { t } = useTranslation();
  const auth = useAuth();
  const settings = useSettings();
  const language = useLanguage();
  const api = useAppointmentService();

  const [doctors, setDoctors] = useState<Doctor[]>([]);
  const [clients, setClients] = useState<Client[]>([]);
  const [schedule, setSchedule] = useState<DoctorDaySchedule | null>(null);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [slotBeingBooked, setSlotBeingBooked] = useState<SlotJson | null>(null);

  const lastDoctorId = useRef<number | null>(null);
  const lastDay = useRef<string | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (auth.isLoggedIn) {
      loadInitialLists();
    }
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
  }, [auth.isLoggedIn]);

  function loadInitialLists(): void {
    api.getAllDoctors().then(setDoctors)
      .catch((err: unknown) => setError(String((err as Error).message ?? err)));
    api.getAllClients().then(setClients)
      .catch((err: unknown) => setError(String((err as Error).message ?? err)));
  }

  function onLogout(): void {
    auth.logOut();
    setDoctors([]); setClients([]); setSchedule(null);
    setError(null); setSlotBeingBooked(null);
    lastDoctorId.current = null; lastDay.current = null;
  }

  function onSearchSchedule(criteria: { doctorId: number; day: string }): void {
    setError(null);
    lastDoctorId.current = criteria.doctorId;
    lastDay.current = criteria.day;
    loadSchedule();
  }

  function onBookingRequest(slot: SlotJson): void {
    setSlotBeingBooked(slot);
  }

  function onConfirmBooking(choice: { clientId: number }): void {
    if (slotBeingBooked === null || lastDay.current === null) {
      return;
    }
    api.addAppointment(lastDay.current, choice.clientId, slotBeingBooked.id)
      .then(() => { setSlotBeingBooked(null); loadSchedule(); })
      .catch((err: unknown) => setError(String((err as Error).message ?? err)));
  }

  function onCancelAppointment(appointment: AppointmentJson): void {
    api.deleteAppointment(appointment.id).then(() => loadSchedule())
      .catch((err: unknown) => setError(String((err as Error).message ?? err)));
  }

  function loadSchedule(): void {
    if (lastDoctorId.current === null || lastDay.current === null) {
      return;
    }
    api.getDoctorScheduleOfDay(lastDoctorId.current, lastDay.current).then(setSchedule)
      .catch((err: unknown) => setError(String((err as Error).message ?? err)));
  }

  return (
    <div className="container py-4">
      <nav className="navbar navbar-expand-sm navbar-dark bg-primary rounded mb-4 px-3">
        <span className="navbar-brand mb-0">{t('APP.TITLE')}</span>
        <div className="d-flex align-items-center gap-2">
          <div className="btn-group btn-group-sm" role="group" aria-label="FR / EN">
            <button type="button" onClick={() => language.changeLanguage('fr')}
              className={'btn ' + (language.currentLanguage === 'fr' ? 'btn-light' : 'btn-outline-light')}>FR</button>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => language.changeLanguage('en')}
              className={'btn ' + (language.currentLanguage === 'en' ? 'btn-light' : 'btn-outline-light')}>EN</button>
          </div>
          {auth.isLoggedIn && (
            <>
              <span className="badge text-bg-light text-primary">{auth.role}</span>
              <span className="text-white">{auth.name}</span>
              <button type="button" className="btn btn-sm btn-outline-light" onClick={onLogout}>
                {t('APP.LOGOUT')}
              </button>
            </>
          )}
        </div>
      </nav>

      <div className="row g-2 align-items-center mb-4">
        <div className="col-auto">
          <label className="form-label mb-0" htmlFor="input-server-url">{t('APP.SERVER_URL_LABEL')}</label>
        </div>
        <div className="col-sm-4">
          <input id="input-server-url" type="text" className="form-control form-control-sm"
            defaultValue={settings.apiBaseUrl} onChange={(e) => settings.setApiBaseUrl(e.target.value)} />
        </div>
      </div>

      {error && <div className="alert alert-danger" role="alert">{error}</div>}

      {!auth.isLoggedIn ? (
        <Login />
      ) : (
        <>
          <DoctorDayPicker doctors={doctors} onSearch={onSearchSchedule} />
          <Schedule schedule={schedule} canEdit={auth.isAdmin}
            onBook={onBookingRequest} onCancel={onCancelAppointment} />
          <BookingDialog open={slotBeingBooked !== null} slot={slotBeingBooked}
            clients={clients} onConfirm={onConfirmBooking} onClose={() => setSlotBeingBooked(null)} />
        </>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 27–28: const lastDoctorId = useRef<number | null>(null); const lastDay = useRef<string | null>(null); — we store the last search (doctor + day) so we can refresh the calendar after a booking or cancellation. A [useRef](), not a [useState](): these two values are never used directly for display (unlike “schedule” or “error”), so there’s no need to redraw the component when they change—exactly the same reasoning that, on the [Angular] side, kept [lastDoctorId/lastDay] as simple private fields rather than signals; Modifying a [useRef]() (.current = …) does not redraw the component, unlike a [setXxx()] from [useState]();
  • lines 30–35: useEffect(() => { if (auth.isLoggedIn) { loadInitialLists(); } }, [auth.isLoggedIn]); — re-executes its body every time [auth.isLoggedIn] changes—the direct equivalent of [effect(() => { if (this.auth.isLoggedIn()) { … } })] on the [Angular] side. It also runs once when the component is mounted: if a session was already stored in [localStorage] (page reload), the lists load immediately upon startup, without waiting for a login;
  • lines 89–94: <div className="btn-group btn-group-sm" …> …FR…EN… </div> — the language selector is visible (including on the login screen); the role badge, name, and logout button, however, are only displayed if [auth.isLoggedIn] (lines 95–103, [{auth.isLoggedIn && (…)})]—exactly the same logic as on the [Angular] and [(@if (auth.isLoggedIn()) { … })] sides;
  • lines 119–130: {!auth.isLoggedIn ? ( <Login /> ): ( <>…</> )} — as long as [useAuth().isLoggedIn] equals false, this component displays only <Login />; since all server routes are now protected by [JwtAuthGuard] (Chapter 3), it would be pointless anyway (and cause 401 errors) to load doctors/clients/calendar before logging in—exactly the same reasoning as for [Angular];
  • lines 123–127: <DoctorDayPicker doctors={doctors} onSearch={onSearchSchedule} /> … — the three “business logic” components from features/ are assembled here, each receiving its props (data + callback functions) — the exact equivalent of the [app.html] template on the [Angular] side, where the same three components appeared with [doctors]="doctors()" ([search)="onSearchSchedule($event)"]….

State ([useState/useRef]), effect ([useEffect]), and event handlers (the onXxx functions): these are exactly the four components already presented in the previous chapter, applied here to the entire root component—nothing new has been introduced in this file; it has simply been assembled.

docs.title: 6.13. What remains out of scope or deferred
docs.text:
The “debug” mode (display of the raw template for the current view) of the original AngularJS 1.x client is a feature deliberately omitted from this port, just as in the [Angular] variant of this course—it will not appear in a later stage of the course (see Chapter 6, Conclusion, for the rationale behind this decision). The setting of an artificial network delay, however, is indeed deferred to a later stage in both variants.

Two additional differences, specific to this [React] port, are worth mentioning here:

  • unit tests (which are absent from this project as well as from the [Angular] project in this course) would follow a different approach in [React]: rather than TestBed (specific to [Angular]), the [React] ecosystem typically relies on [React Testing Library]—not presented in this document;
  • type checking for templates ([Angular] strictTemplates, see previous chapter) has no equivalent that needs to be configured separately on the [React] side: it is the TypeScript compiler itself that checks the [JSX], just like any other .tsx file—a simplification of the configuration, at the cost, in theory, of slightly less deep integration between the template language and the type system (in practice, on this project, no observable difference).

docs.title: 7.1. What Was Built
docs.text:
This document has adapted the functional core and authentication of the [RdvMedecins] application from the original 2014 document to current technologies:

  • a complete [NestJS] server ([TypeORM] entities, DAO, business layer, web layer), exposing the same 11 business routes (JSON) as the original Spring 4 server, on the same port (8080), all now protected by a token (JWT);
  • an authentication layer ([@nestjs/passport] + [@nestjs/jwt]): login/password authentication (POST /login), a signed token presented with each subsequent request, and role-based access control ([@Roles]('ADMIN') + [RolesGuard]) on the two routes that modify data;
  • a [React] client (functional components, hooks) offering the same features as the original AngularJS 1.x client—selecting a doctor and a date, viewing the calendar, booking and canceling an appointment - supplemented with a login screen, a persistent session (localStorage), a Bootstrap interface that adapts to the logged-in user’s role (booking buttons hidden for a specific role), and the ability to switch the interface between French and English ([i18next] + [react-i18next]).

The core of the database has not changed (same tables [doctors/clients/slots/appointments], same constraints), except for the addition of the table [users]; nor has the general layered architecture—only the tools that implement it have been updated.

There are two intentional differences from the authentication method in the original document, documented in detail in Chapter 3: a JWT token rather than the HTTP Basic header sent with each request, and a single [role] column per user rather than a many-to-many relationship across three tables. A third difference—this one functional—was deliberately chosen for this port: the USER role can now view calendars (read-only), whereas in the original it served only to illustrate a total denial of access.

docs.title: 7.2. What Remains Outside the Scope or to Be Ported
docs.text: Beyond the above, the original document covered three additional topics—one of which has now been addressed, another deliberately left out, and the third deferred to a later stage:

docs.title: 7.2.1. French/English localization—addressed in this document
docs.text: The original document proposed switching the interface between French and English using the [angular-translate] library. This port implements this functionality using its equivalent in the current [React] ecosystem, [i18next] (along with [react-i18next], which loads the dictionaries fr.json/en.json with HTTP from the [public/i18n/] folder)—see Chapter 5. Like [angular-translate] before it, [i18next] allows you to switch languages on the fly, without reloading the page—a behavior faithful to that of the original document.

docs.title: 7.2.2. The client’s “debug” mode—deliberately excluded from the scope
docs.text: The original document included a technical display mode, activatable from the interface, which provided access to the raw model ($scope AngularJS 1.x) of the current view—a useful feature in 2014, when the development tools available for inspecting a AngularJS application were still limited. This port does not recreate it: current [React] development tools ([React] DevTools, official browser extension) now offer, outside of the application itself, a much more comprehensive inspection of components, their state (hooks), and their props than a custom debugging panel reintegrated into the interface would provide. Adding such a panel would amount to creating a lesser version of a tool already provided by the ecosystem—this decision is therefore final, not merely a postponement.

docs.title: 7.2.3. Artificial network delay—postponed
docs.text: The original document allowed setting an artificial delay before each server response, to observe the interface’s behavior on a slow network (loading indicators, temporary button deactivation, etc.). This feature does not yet have an equivalent in this port.

docs.title: 7.3. A note on the methodology used in this document
docs.text: This document was written based entirely on the code that was actually executed: every server path was tested (including authentication scenarios: successful/failed login, access without a token, access with the wrong role), and every client screenshot (Chapter 5) was obtained by interacting with the actual running application—an automatically controlled Chromium browser using demo data from the provided SQL script. This approach also revealed, during the preparation of this document, a specific issue regarding the use of [TypeORM] with calculated columns ([@RelationId])—which was reported and corrected in Chapter 3, directly in the delivered code. This requirement also explains why Postman screenshots are not included in this document: rather than simulating them, it seemed preferable to leave this step to the document’s author, who can create them directly from their own workstation.

docs.title: 7.4. To Get Started Right Away
docs.text:
While waiting for the next steps in this port, the server and client included with this document provide a ready-to-use foundation for you to experiment on your own:

  • add a new doctor or a new patient (currently, this can only be done by modifying the SQL script—a route named /addDoctor, also protected by [@Roles]('ADMIN'), could be a good first exercise);
  • add a third role, or a user with multiple roles—an opportunity to assess, in very concrete terms, the cost of abandoning the single-column simplification [role] (see Chapter 3);
  • modify the client’s presentation (colors, layout) without changing the server—a good way to verify that the client’s layered architecture works as intended;
  • Review the README file for each folder in the delivered server and client: each explains, in its context, the role of the files it contains.

docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s AI Claude. Its purpose is to transpose the document [A Client/Server Example - AngularJS 1.x / Spring 4] in two ways:

  • the client AngularJS 1.x is replaced by a client [React] 19;
  • the Java web framework Spring MVC is replaced by the web framework NestJS;

Claude from Anthropic (AI) did most of the work (90%):

  • code generation: Claude generated all of the code. I simply tested it by following the generated course;
  • Course generation in the ODT format: Claude generated several versions at my request. This is where I was primarily involved.

Note 1: If the reader’s primary goal is to “learn NestJS,” a simpler example is available in the [Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Web Framework by Example] document. The reader can then return to this document to understand the React client library.

Note 2: This document frequently refers to version [Angular] of this course. This refers to course [A Client/Server Example - Angular / NestJS (2026)];

Serge Tahé, September 2026

==

This document is a follow-up to the course “A Client/Server Example - AngularJS 1.x / Spring 4,” written in 2014. That original document built a small medical appointment scheduling application (“[RdvMedecins]”) using a Spring 4 / Spring Data / Spring MVC server and a AngularJS 1.x client.

Twelve years later, the two frameworks used have evolved significantly—or have even been replaced in common use:

  • on the server side, [NestJS] has established itself as one of the most widely used Node.js/TypeScript frameworks for building structured web applications, with a philosophy similar to that of Spring (modules, controllers, services, dependency injection) but within the JavaScript/TypeScript ecosystem;
  • on the client side, AngularJS 1.x were completely rewritten starting in 2016 under the name [Angular] (versions 2, 4, 5… up to version 22) - the approach taken by the [Angular] / [NestJS] variant in this course. This document takes a different, more radical approach: [React] (created by Meta, 2013), an interface library rather than a complete framework, in which each component is a simple function JavaScript/TypeScript (see Chapter 4).

The purpose of this document is to revisit the original case study—the same application, the same features, the same database—and to rebuild it using current tools, while maintaining, as much as possible, the same instructional progression as the 2014 document.

docs.title: 1.1. A Step-by-Step Reconstruction
docs.text:
The original document was about 300 pages long and covered, in addition to the application’s core functionality—role-based authentication (Spring Security)—twelve progressive examples for learning AngularJS 1.x step by step. Reconstructing all of this content at once would be both time-consuming and difficult to digest.

This document therefore covers the first two steps of the reconstruction:

  • the application’s general architecture (unchanged in principle);
  • the database (unchanged, except for the addition of the [users] table);
  • the complete [NestJS] server, with all features for viewing and booking/canceling appointments;
  • token-based authentication (JWT) and role-based access control (ADMIN/USER), equivalent to the Spring Security layer in the original document;
  • the corresponding [React] client, with the same features, a login screen, a Bootstrap interface tailored to the logged-in user’s role, and the ability to switch the interface between French and English ([i18next]/[react-i18next]).

Two features from the original document are not included in this document at this stage: the original client’s “debug” mode (display of the raw template for the current view), which has been deliberately omitted from this port (see Chapter 6 for the rationale behind this decision), and the configuration of an artificial network delay, which has been deferred to a later stage.

docs.title: 1.2. Who This Document Is Intended For
docs.text:
This document assumes no prior knowledge of either [NestJS] or [React]. Each new concept (decorator, dependency injection, component, hook, etc.) is explained as it appears, in as much detail as possible—even for readers who have never written a single line of TypeScript.

However, some basic knowledge is helpful for getting the most out of this document:

  • a basic understanding of the JavaScript language (variables, functions, arrays, objects);
  • a basic understanding of HTTP interactions in a web application (GET/POST methods, JSON format);
  • common tags in the HTML language;
  • using the command line (cd, npm install…).

You do not need to be familiar with the TypeScript language (used on both the server and client sides) beforehand: it is a superset of JavaScript that adds a type system, which is explained throughout the document whenever it is used. Interested readers may consult the [Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Framework (2026)] document, which explains TypeScript in detail.

docs.title: 1.3. The Application Architecture
docs.text:
The general architecture of the application has not changed since the original document:

  • a web server delivers a single HTML/a unique CSS/JS page, containing a [React] application built on the Component model (view + associated logic), which relies on services to communicate with the server;
  • the user interacts with the views displayed in the browser. The user’s actions sometimes require a request to the server [NestJS], which processes the request and returns a response JSON (JavaScript Object Notation); this response is used to update the view presented to the user.

The application under consideration will have the following architecture:

  • In [1], the user of the [React] application queries the [presentation] layer [2] of that application;
  • to perform the action requested by the user, the [presentation] layer [2] may query the [Services] layer [3];
  • To provide the requested service, the [3] layer may need to query [4], the remote server JSON implemented by [NestJS];
  • Depending on the request received in [5], the [6-8] layers may be queried;
  • the server’s response returns the [2-8] layers in reverse order;
  • the view displayed to the user, [1], reflects this response;

Note: If you’re confused by the project’s architecture, refer back to this diagram. Note that DBMS is processed by the server, not by the client.

docs.title: 1.4. Tools Used
docs.text:
This document uses the following tools (their installation is detailed in Chapter 1):

  • Node.js (version 22 or later) and its package manager npm—the equivalent, in the JavaScript ecosystem, of what Java + Maven were for the original Spring server;
  • Visual Studio Code, a free code editor, with its TypeScript extensions—the equivalent of Spring Tool Suite (STS) and WebStorm used in the original document;
  • [NestJS] CLI ([@nestjs/cli]), a command-line tool that generates the server project structure and launches its development server; On the client side, [Vite] requires no global installation—it can be used directly via npm on the project included with this document;
  • [MySQL] 8 for the database (the original document used [MySQL] 5—the relational schema itself remains unchanged);
  • Postman (or any other HTTP client), to test the server’s URL that respond to POST requests (/addAppointment, /deleteAppointment)—a browser can only test GET requests.

docs.title: 1.5. Application Features
docs.text:
The “business” features of the [RdvMedecins] application remain unchanged from the original document; access control, however, is slightly more robust than in the original (see the table below):

  • A medical practice employs several doctors, each with their own consultation time slots;
  • a user must log in (username/password) to access the application;
  • Once logged in, the user can select a doctor and a day, and view the doctor’s schedule for that day: each time slot appears either available or booked;
  • a user with the role ADMIN can also book an available time slot for a patient of their choice and cancel an existing appointment;
  • A user with the role USER can view the schedules but cannot book or cancel (read-only access)—a deliberate difference from the original document, where the role USER was used solely to illustrate a denial of access and could not view anything at all (see Chapter 3, “Authentication” section, for the rationale behind this choice).

docs.title: 1.7. Organization of this document
docs.text:
1. Setting up the development environment—installing the tools, creating the database, and launching the server and client for the first time.
  1. Introduction to [NestJS]—the basics of the framework (modules, controllers, providers), with a mini-project to get started.
  2. The [NestJS] server for the [RdvMedecins] application—the database, the [TypeORM] entities, the DAO layer, the business layer, the web layer, and token-based authentication (JWT) and roles.
  3. Introduction to [React]—the basics of the library (functional components, JSX, hooks, Context), with a review of concepts already covered on the [Angular] side.
  4. The [React] client for the [RdvMedecins] application—the client architecture, each of its components (including the login screen), the Bootstrap interface, switching between French and English in the interface, and a step-by-step walkthrough of the complete application.
  5. Conclusion and Next Steps.
